speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will just wait for the applause to die down a little before I have my chance for the last kick at the cat on Bill C-12. We have debated this matter at some length, and I suspect that the Bill will finally be dealt with today and hence go to the Senate for final approval and Royal Assent. After that the chickens will come home to roost, undoubtedly, in the educational community across Canada.
The Bill itself, as we have discovered during the course of debate, is extremely complex. It contains mathematical formulae which are unintelligible to me and I assume to most other people who have looked at it. If we look into what the Bill really does, it becomes quite apparent. Its objective is to cut down the amount of money being made available by the federal Government for institutions of higher learning, money which would have been funnelled through the provinces into universities and like institutions.
What is the quantity of funds which will be taken out of educational budgets? If we look at the Bill, we find that in the 1983-84 fiscal year the cutback is to be in the amount of $118 million. For the year thereafter, the 1984-85 fiscal year, the cutback will be even larger, some $260 million. The worst fears of the provinces are being realized.
Several years ago the provinces became trapped into these types of cost-shared programs with the federal Government.
The federal Government, at that time flush with funds because the economy of Canada was in much better shape than it is today, gave the provinces an offer they could not refuse. They sucked them in. It said that for every dollar they spent on some kind of approved program, it would give them 50 cents. The provinces had been pretty happy before. They had funded things in their constitutional jurisdiction out of taxes they were able to impose. Along comes the federal Government with the objective of having a reasonable degree of standardization across the country and offers them these extra moneys. Of course, any province which did not take advantage of that program was unable to compete with the provinces that did. However, what they lost in this exercise was flexibility. Medical care expenses, hospital care expenses and higher education expenses were no longer subject to changes to be made at the provincial level. There was always this federal influence. They lost flexibility and they lost control over areas which under our Constitution were mainly within their domain. They just could not refuse to accept that money even if they would have liked to do so.
Then what happens when times get tough? Times are pretty tough right now. I suspect they will remain tough as long as we have a Liberal Government in office. The first area the federal Government looks to to cut back expenses is in the cost-shared areas, such as higher education, as we see in this Bill, medical care and hospital insurance, as we have seen previously. It says it will withdraw money from those areas. Then the provinces, who are the deliverers of the services, will get the political blame when students cannot enrol in universities, when people cannot get the medical care to which they feel in a country like Canada they should be entitled.
It is easy for the federal Government to cut back in these areas because it is not the deliverer of the services or the programs. It is the provinces which do that. The federal Government expects that the political flak, the distaste of the electorate, will be shown against the provinces rather than against it. The provinces in these matters have been left holding the bag.
Yesterday I was fortunate to participate in a very interesting meeting with representatives of the Canadian Association of University Teachers. It was a most worth-while exercise. I learned a great deal at that meeting talking with the representatives of the university teachers across this country. At the meeting we were told of the low morale that permeates universities and their teachers. Most of this can be attributed to the lack of funds for teachers. They told us that teaching in universities is suffering in many cases as a result of federal

Established Programs Financing cutbacks. They told us that research efforts in Canadian universities are also suffering because money is not available for that purpose.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) and other members of the Treasury benches tell us how excited they are about the new age in Canada. I believe they call it the new information age. They tell us that there is a need for a highly trained workforce in Canada. If we as a country are to survive in the forthcoming years, we have to be highly literate. When Canadians come out of schools and universities and take up some kind of profession, they should not in the future feel that they are in that one particular job indefinitely. There will be a need for continuous education, continuous training throughout their lives. As one job disappears and another comes on to the scene, it will be easy for people to transfer from one task to another.
We have to look at a different concept of the labour force in years to come. If we do not do these things, we will lose out on the modern world toward the end of this century and into the next. If we do not devote sufficient attention and resources- financial, human and otherwise-to these training needs, we will not survive as a trading nation. We will not be able to sustain the high standard of living which we previously enjoyed in Canada.
We asked the Canadian Association of University Teachers how much money we were talking about. We asked whether it was a billion dollars, which is not that much today. We wanted to know how much they were talking about, what level of funding would solve their problems. The answer was rather surprising, and it was really not all that much money. The answer was $280 million. That would seem to be a large amount of money to some people. However, it can be contrasted with the billion and a half dollars that went to bail out Canadair. It can be contrasted with the $350 million that was given to de Havilland the other day to save just a few jobs, and I do not think it will even do that because those jobs will be fast disappearing. The amount of money required is not that great.
From the more than $80 billion of federal expenditures, it would not, in my opinion, be too difficult to find $280 million to invest in higher education. That money does not have to be found by increasing taxation or increasing the deficit but can be found by priorizing expenditures. If we did not find ourselves in these bail-out schemes which get worse and worse as they go along and never seem to end, and if we did not have to devote the resources of Canada, through taxes on gasoline, to Petro-Canada so that it could buy out Petrofina but instead invested that money in higher education, we would be much better off down the road.
There was another point brought to our attention by the Canadian Association of University Teachers and I would like to touch upon it just briefly. The association mentioned the difficulty it has with governments, both provincial and federal, when universities wish to put their own houses in order. If
those charged with the financial administration of a university, realizing the difficult straits in which they find themselves, wish to rationalize their own affairs and discover how they can put available moneys to better use, they find that because of complex funding arrangements with governments they are unable to put their plans into effect.
We were told, for instance, that a certain university might desire to close down a small department in which there is not a great deal of interest or a great many students. There would obviously be the need for training in that particular area but perhaps a university nearby would specialize in that field. If a university wished to close down a certain department and use some of the funds that were saved thereby in another department in which it has expertise and for which there is a great deal of demand, it is not possible to do so because of financial arrangements with the funding bodies. If the university cuts out that one department, then all of the funding that went to that department is taken away. The universities are not able to rationalize sensibly. I believe there is a greater need for flexible arrangements in the financial field between the provincial governments and universities so that this type of thing does not happen.
When we were dealing with second reading of this Bill, I gave a presentation which went into a fair amount of detail about the effect of the tax system in Canada on university financing. I do not wish to go into it again but, because I feel it is a very important point, I would like to mention it briefly in passing. In the past, a great deal of private money went to universities. People tended to endow things like chairs to universities or make donations. However, because the Canadian tax system almost forbids the accumulation of private wealth, that no longer takes place.
If one were to speak to financial administrators of universities, one would find that, by and large, most of their money, even a portion of that which comes by way of tuition fees, comes from the federal Government, the provincial governments and in the form of research grants. Invariably, it comes from government. They are becoming almost exclusively dependent on state financing. I continue to consider that to be a most dangerous trend. I do not think there is anything particularly wrong with government funding of universities, but they should also have operating funds coming from elsewhere. Otherwise, while I do not think it will be today since the Government, as bad as it is, has not yet tried directly to influence hiring and firing in universities and to tell university professors what to think, it should be kept in mind that eventually this could very well happen in future unless universities retain some degree of independence.
When it comes to the role of the state in university financing, I think it does have a role. There has always been a role. If one looks at it in a historical context, monarchs of old have secured for themselves everlasting fame and a place in the history books by their support of universities and institutes of higher learning. It has always been the case that the govern-
April 12, 1984

ment of the day or, in past times, a particular queen or king has been remembered for their support in the founding of institutions of the nature we are talking about. They have been remembered for their continued support of them and for the bringing together of expertise into one establishment.
As well, when one looks at it in a historical context, it will be seen that something that might have been done in the year 1500 did not really pay dividends until 1595 or some 100 years down the road. It is the same in Canada today. We must continue to support our universities in order that 50 or 100 years from now Canada can still hold its head upright in the affairs of nations. I am afraid that the Government may well go down in the history books not as a body of people who have supported education to the end that things might improve 50 years hence, but as a group that has neglected that important field of human endeavour.
Now, in the brief minutes that remain to me I want to touch very quickly on three issues of local concern to me in the Northwest Territories. My first concern is the problem we are having with adult education in the communities. For some time, orginally as a government initiatives, we have tried to provide the opportunity for adults, many of whom have never gone to school or only to grade three, four or five, with the opportunity to become literate and take the jobs that are coming as economic development becomes more available in northern Canada. We are having some problems with the funding thereof. In my opinion, it is something that should get a high degree of priority if we are not, in northern Canada, to have a large proportion of our population put aside, unable to take advantage of the many opportunities that are coming forward, particularly in the resource exploitation field.
We have in the Territories one institution of higher learning, Thebacha College. It is having problems with the amount of money made available to it. I wanted to bring out one particular area of concern which it is experiencing now and that is with its library. There is a very nice college, with some excellent staff, but it is a little short on books. If any Hon. Members who are listening can think of a way that we can bring some books to our library at Thebacha College in Forth Smith, Northwest Territories, I can assure them that they would have the absolute support and gratitude of the staff and students attending that institution. Perhaps someone could find a university that has a collection of books since we do not have books and would like to become a university.
My final point deals with the teaching of the French language in the Northwest Territories. A Bill was introduced in this House, unilaterally, I might add, and I have some doubts about its value and worth, which I will not get into now. The effect of this Bill, if it goes through, will be to make the Yukon and Northwest Territories officially bilingual, whether or not that is a good idea. It will cost a lot of money to do this. All the Hansards of the legislature will have to be translated at great public expense. All the ordinances and regulations will have to be translated. The operation of the courts will become

very difficult and expensive. There will be a lot of money needed for that.
But, believe it or not, students who want to learn French in the high schools are unable to do so because they cannot raise another $50,000 or so to hire a French teacher. There are a couple of high schools that have had this very problem. They have not been able to get French teachers to teach these students who want to learn French. Yet the Government can come into Parliament with a Bill prepared to spend millions and millions of dollars translating dry documents going back to the time of Rupert's Land. That, in my opinion, does not make any sense whatsoever.

I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, that that question was asked. The observations of the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) are excellent, Sir. We should be working towards the establishment of a full university in Canada's north. It is not something which can be done overnight. We can use existing institutions such as Thebacha College which I have already mentioned, the college with no books, as a base. We can make arrangements with existing southern universities to come up to the north, perhaps have a university college there and work in association with territorial institutions. Perhaps the first year or first two years of a university course could be given in the north; then the students would again have to go south. However, we must work towards this idea of the establishment of a university in the north. It is not something which can be done overnight but it is something which we are and definitely should be working toward. I believe the opportunities there, both on the teaching side and the research side, are excellent and I would like to see this trend continue.
We have had some problems with southern universities which previously were most pleased to be able to take students from the north, particularly those universities in Alberta and some in Montreal and Quebec. Now, however, because of the cutbacks in funding, they are becoming much more parochial and are saying: "We only have so much money; we should concentrate on taking students from Alberta or Quebec", and so on. They are much more reluctant to allow territorial students who have no universities of their own to go to those southern institutions. So that is definitely a problem.
With respect to the final point of the question, the use of modern technology for educational purposes, this will come, probably not so much for university programs, but it will allow us to give a lot of basic literacy courses and vocational-type training in remote communities without the people having to

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak at the third reading stage of a Bill which, when implemented, will limit increases to 6 per cent for the first year and 5 per cent for this year in the amounts the federal Government contributes to post-secondary education. It is obvious that the Government is determined to implement this policy with no amendment, retraction or remorse for the damage it is inflicting on an educational system already in crisis.
This is not the only Bill which will accomplish that. A few weeks ago the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) announced what amounted to a reduction in funding to postgraduate programs administered through the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. I am sure the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will try to impose the same kind of limits on the education of young native people for which it is legally responsible. These limits come at a time when we have 1.5 million unemployed, probably 40 per cent of whom are young people.
As a result of this large scale unemployment, our universities and community colleges have been flooded with applications for enrolment. It had been assumed that, because of the declining birth rate which began some 20 years ago, the number of students wishing to attend universities and community colleges would decline. In fact, the number of those who want to attend is at an all-time high. At the same time the federal Government decides for purely financial reasons, not because it has looked at the need for education, to limit the amount of money it will provide to help fund post-secondary education. This Bill will have a very serious effect not only on post-secondarty education, but on all education. The provinces share in the cost of post-secondary education and they will now have to try to meet some of the shortfall in funding caused by these limitations. One way of doing that is to be very careful, cautious and hard on the elementary and high school systems for which they have the responsibility.
All of this comes at a time, Mr. Speaker, when, because of new technologies, our educational system has to be revamped to help those who have lost or will lose their jobs because of automation. That is the time that the federal Government picks to get tough. In addition to those people, Mr. Speaker, there are whole groups in our society who have been shortchanged through our educational system's failure to meet their needs. Let me just indicate a few of the groups who have real trouble.
We have had hundreds of thousands of immigrants who have come to Canada in the last 15 or 20 years whose language is neither English nor French. They have been encouraged to come to this country because of the policies put
forward by the federal Government, a Liberal Government for 19 of those 20 years. We find those people in big cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver. Our school systems have found that the children from these families where the first language is not English or French, in order to fit into our society and play a useful role, need more teachers and teaching aids, new kinds of text books. Special efforts have to be made and extra costs are incurred. But at the same time the federal and provincial governments are saying to them: "We cannot afford to help you".
According to a number of studies we have several million people who are functionally illiterate. Those people are not finding and will not be able to find good jobs. Even when the economy improves, they will not be able to find jobs in the new technological age. There are really no programs on the part of the federal of provincial governments, so far as I can tell, which deal with the problem of those people. When the federal Government says it is going to put a cap on the money it spends for education, Mr. Speaker, that means we are writing those people off.
The last group I want to speak about, Mr. Speaker, is our native people. The education of many of our native people, including those now attending school, is at about the level they would get in a Third World country. There has been some improvement; native children are attending schools longer and getting higher grades than they did 10 or 20 years ago. But the number of native children who graduate from our high schools can be numbered at a few thousand, I am sure. I have seen some studies which indicate that in many areas in Manitoba- and I am sure it is the same in many other provinces-not one single native student from a reserve will finish high school. What are we doing about that? Very little. When we put a cap on our spending on education, we are writing those people off. That is not acceptable to me and it should not be acceptable to any person who cares about people in this country.
In this rapidly changing environment of computerization and information technology, the pressure is on the primary and secondary school system to integrate with the new technology and prepare this generation of children for the implications of the changes taking place. What are we saying when we limit our contributions to post-secondary education? We are accepting that we are not going to face the problem. We say the Government should provide special capital grants to enable financially strapped school boards to consider offering computer-related programs which they do not now offer. We New Democrats, Mr. Speaker, are not noted for believing in tax concessions.
[DOT] (U40)
However, I would suggest a practical option is to change the tax system so that corporations could donate appropriate equipment to schools. That would be a practical way of helping the schools meet their problems. Both the above measures could apply equally to vocational and technical colleges, high schools and polytechnical facilities which, due to the recession and Bills such as the one we are dealing with
April 12, 1984

today, are attempting to train for the future with obsolete, outdated equipment.
Originally the federal Government provided capital grants to assist in constructing and equipping these institutions. In a period of rapid technological change it is not unreasonable that the federal Government should show some leadership and concern and provide for the renewal of some of the equipment in these institutions, so that they can do the type of jobs they are supposed to do. They were set up to a large extent with federal funding. In order for them to do the job they are supposed to do, they must have the proper equipment, otherwise they can only fail.
It seems to me that the guiding principle of the Government in matters of education is to cut and slash. It wants to minimize its involvement and concern in order that the allimportant deficit be reduced. Meanwhile federal budgets heap more and more tax breaks on the multinationals and conglomerates that the Government looks up to for leadership. The tax system permits the wealthiest individuals to pay little or no taxes. We know, Mr. Speaker, that more than 250 people who had incomes of more than $250,000 paid no income tax in the last year for which we have figures. We know there were over 7,000 people who had incomes of over $50,000 who paid no income tax in the last year for which we have figures. I suggest that an equitable tax system would do away with the necessity for the kinds of restrictions which the Government is proposing in this Bill.
The attack on educational and social programs by both the Liberal and Conservative Parties, both here in Ottawa and in the provinces, is going to have a disastrous effect on the lives of the people of this country. The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) has attacked the Government for the deficit which we face. This comes at the same time as he and his colleagues are calling almost every day for the Government to inaugurate new programs to help the farmers, the fishermen and other groups. There is not much honesty in that type of approach as far as I am concerned. One of the candidates in the Liberal leadership race, Mr. Turner, is basing his candidacy on a pledge to further cut the deficit. I suggest that, in effect, means lowering the level of social and educational services which we have provided in the country.
The major problem with the Government is that it has lost touch with the people it is sworn to serve. In the City of Toronto, for instance, there are 55,000 young unemployed Canadians. A substantial number of them are skilled, but have the wrong skills to meet the demand for jobs that are available. Statistics Canada reports that there are some 540,000 young Canadians who are unemployed and looking for work. This is almost double the official unemployment rate for the nation. This represents a staggering cost of billions of dollars of lost productivity which we will never recover. Some estimates have indicated that the total number of unemployed youth is not the 540,000 young Canadians that Statistics Canada reports, but that in fact at least 200,000 more young people have given up their search for a job because there just are not any.
Established Programs Financing
It does not make sense for the Government to be cutting back on federal funding for post-secondary education at a time when such a crisis of unemployment for young people has exploded across this country. Officials in the core areas of our cities where the poor and unemployed tend to live have noticed an increase in vandalism, petty crime, prostitution, shoplifting and breaking and entering. These officials feel that such events can only signal deeper social unrest in the months ahead. The apparent reaction of the Government is the Bill before the House today which cuts back on the services I have indicated. This will only accentuate the difficulties I have alluded to.
Why does the Government persist in this policy? I can only guess that the Liberal Government has lost sight of the effects which these cuts can and will have and has no strategy for implementing real solutions through the educational system, whether it be vocational training, skills retraining, secondary school orientation for career paths or post-secondary specialization and post-graduate support. Federal Government education support and manpower training are not now geared to any over-all strategy or vision of the future. Despite a number of studies which have been made that indicated clearly that the Department of Employment and Immigration should make a bigger effort to deal with the lack of education and the illiteracy which I referred to earlier, the Department has allocated less and less funds for training those kinds of people in recent years rather than making a bigger effort.
The effects of cuts such as will take place as a result of passage of this Bill will be evident if we examine what is happening in the provinces. I think all Members know the difficulties which are arising in the Province of Ontario. The universities and community colleges have been told that they must cut back on the expenditures, that they cannot meet the needs of their students and that they are going to have to limit the number of students they can accept for training and education. The clearest indication of what happens when the federal Government or the provinces decide to hold the line, or in fact to cut back on educational funding, can be seen in the Province of British Columbia. That province has used the cuts in federal funding for post-secondary education as a justification of its own efforts to slash support for universal access to education and diverse educational programs geared to meet the needs of the workforce. In British Columbia less than 10 per cent of the student age population is in university or other post-secondary institutions. The figure for all of Canada is 12.68 per cent while the Japanese rate is 40 per cent and the U.S. rate is 20 per cent.
Can we look forward to anything, Mr. Speaker, other than a situation in which Canada will fall further behind other modern industrialized countries in meeting the needs of the new technology? This Bill does exactly the wrong thing. This Bill will create a situation which will have adverse disastrous effects, and not just in 1984, 1985 and 1986. The tremendously serious effects of these cutbacks and reductions will be felt in this country for generations to come. It is for those reasons, Mr. Speaker, that we oppose this Bill.

April 12, 1984
Established Programs Financing

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on this Bill has gone on for some time. It brings out many of the problems in Canada today, namely lack of consultation between the federal Government and the provincial governments. This is a serious situation in which the Liberals have placed us. The Liberals have taken Bill C-12 and they have tried to say: "Because of our six and five program we have to reduce the expenditure for education". If the Liberals had made an honest attempt to work out the problem with the provinces- because education is a provincial responsibility-then they could have possibly stayed with the six and five. To me, Mr. Speaker, it is shocking that the Government can increase its own spending by in excess of 11 per cent on salaries and by many more per cent in different directions, yet on the most important subject in modern Canada, what do we have?
Education must be addressed. Many speakers have referred to higher education and specifically to universities. That is just one segment. There is another major segment and that is the retraining of Canadians-retraining and retraining. People will possibly go through a retraining program four or five times during their lives. Universities are not the only vehicle. We must develop more community colleges. We must develop more trade schools. We must get co-operation with industry. Today is the day we must encourage people to become more knowledgeable and more literate both in language and in computer technology.
I have spoken before on this Bill and I speak on it again because there are many more points to be made. For instance,
I heard the red rump going on in the same direction about tax credits.

speechtext:
The Government cannot afford what we are doing now under present circumstances. The only way this country can be turned around is to get the economy turned around. In that way, if the Government provided the same percentage of GNP and the GNP was higher, then the education program problem would not be serious. But we must address the importance of education in Canada today. Without co-operation with the provinces, that will never happen.
I would like to recommend to the Government that it sit down with each province individually and try to work out the needs of each province. If the Government works out the needs with each province and then holds a federal-provincial meeting to get consensus on the importance of education in Canada today, this would be helpful.
We brought down a task force report last weekend that was probably one of the most brilliant pieces of literature that I have had the opportunity to read. It brought forth the problems that Canada would face in the next 20 years. That first 20 years will move into 50 years. We are at a critical stage. We did not address this problem soon enough, as the Japanese did and as the Americans have. The Japanese, for example, were aware of the problem back in the 1960s. They built up their institutions and education to a level that could compensate for new technology and get people trained so they could fit into that requirement.
New technology is not the only criteria, Mr. Speaker. We have to deal with Canadians and give Canadians encouragement. Because of our deficit, there is little room for the Government to manoeuvre. I accept that. The only way out of that is by increasing the GNP.
I suggest that the Government bring in equity in taxation credits for education. An example that was recently brought to my attention was an article in the newspaper. The article was written about a young lady registered at McGill who took some of her courses at another university. She did that to fit into the program in which she wanted to become proficient. Because of that, Revenue Canada denied her the opportunity of deducting her expense against her income. I am not necessarily talking about deductions for students because students have such a hard time earning any income this day and age when there is such a shortage of work. I am talking about parents of students.
I recall that when I was young a life insurance salesman approached me when my first son was born and asked me if I would like to take out an insurance policy on him. My first reaction was that I did not want to benefit from my son's death. The salesman then explained to me it was an education program and that by putting so much money per month into this insurance program I could guarantee my son an education. That is forward thinking. We had that 30 years ago. Today we are looking from day to day, going from brink to brink, and we
April 12, 1984

have to stop. We have to start dealing with the long-term problem.
I believe we should provide some form of a program, such as the RHOSP, whereby parents can put money aside after a child is born and during his lifetime in order to create a fund to provide education. But I would go beyond that and say that parents should also be allowed to put funds aside to create a program for retraining themselves. We are in a critical stage. We must address the problem of my peers and the younger people who will be getting into our peers' age group in a few years. They will have to put money aside and they cannot afford to do so after taxes. We must do something about this. If the Government cannot provide for proper funding, then the individual will have to provide more of the funding. In order for the individual to do that, he must be given the incentive to do so.
The key point I am trying to make is that we must encourage Canadians to be productive. We must encourage them to become involved in the voluntary sector and different industries. However, we are discouraging Canadians; the great master state is now looking after them from cradle to grave. We have to overcome this and encourage people to help themselves.
Grants are given for new buildings and new institutions. There are a number of churches across Canada with basements that are not fully utilized. Those basements could be used for computer training at night or during the day, but no, the state wants total control. On that subject alone, some churches and other bodies have voluntary organizations and charge a fee for people to learn a new trade. Under the Unemployment Insurance Act a man is denied taking a fulltime course at one of these institutions unless he will commit himself to the fact that, if so required, he will drop his schooling and return to the job. It is far more valuable for a person, rather than taking a temporary, part-time job, to be retrained in something which will provide him with a life-long skill. If we put a deterrent in the way of that gentleman, we are being totally unfair to the Canadian public. It is things such as that in the Income Tax Act which are forcing the Government to be the big daddy who will look after us and do everything for us. We must create an incentive for Canadians to help themselves. The Government must lead the way but it has not done so.
Many times in committee NDP members stated that the provinces were not keeping up their contributions. There is a way of dealing with that, and that is consultation. If after consultation they still refuse to increase their expenditure in education, then we can deal with it and participate on an even basis with the provinces. If we do that, the provinces will get smart very quickly because it is important to them to have funding.
In these times when we have gone through tremendous deficits, all provinces have competed with the federal Government to see who could be the biggest spender. One province in
Established Programs Financing particular has been attacked on this point, the Province of British Columbia. Perhaps some of the things it has done have been too radical, but its intention was to reduce expenditures and ultimately reduce the provincial deficit. Provinces cannot afford any more than the federal Government can afford.
Again I say that the problem is critical. If we do not provide funding through the federal Government for training and retraining, we will continue having 1.5 million people unemployed who, according to the information I have been given from many sources, are costing our economy $50 billion. If a portion of that $50 billion was put into training, retraining and education, we would not only solve the unemployment problem but the problem which was brought to my attention last week by Mr. Fred Pomeroy, Vice-President of the CLC. He stated that we had to go abroad to bring in personnel to work in areas of new technology because we were bankrupt in the field. He said that we have not properly trained people for the upcoming high technology. Labour is on our side on this point. It is concerned and sick of Canada always depending upon bringing new people into the country to solve problems. We have approximately 25 million Canadians. Surely to God we can provide the training required for the new technology. We are not doing it. The Government is not addressing it and this Bill does not address it.
I have spoken in the House many times against Government spending on Crown corporations, particularly de Havilland and Canadair, which has amounted to some $5 billion that could have been put into education and would have probably reduced unemployment by at least a third. It is a shocking situation. Something has to be done.
We have to call for a national strategy to deal with the post-secondary educational system. The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, in a report by Dr. Symons and Dr. James Page, indicated very clearly that this matter must be discussed because it is of critical importance. Furthermore, the universities are shocked because they must recruit teachers from overseas. Again, with 25 million people in the country, we cannot provide adequate teachers to teach our own students! Visiting professors from other countries is a great idea, but they should be just that, visiting professors to assist our own people to upgrade their teaching skills and their knowledge of the new technology. This report is of critical importance. It is totally non-partisan, but no one in the Party opposite has indicated that a meeting will take place to develop a national strategy to deal with post-secondary education.
Also I would like to point out the importance of communications with the provinces. There is a weakness in the system before the post-secondary education stage. Some of the present costs are for upgrading student skills in English and basic arithmetic. I have talked to people involved in the universities about this and they maintain that part of the trouble is that everything is based on the GPA-the average mark. Some people are experts in mathematics, some are experts in English. A young man who may want to go into physics and maths may obtain 100 per cent in those subjects, but he may be excluded from the course because of a weakness in language

April 12, 1984
Established Programs Financing
skills. We have to address this problem. We have to provide for such people. They are the geniuses, the brains and the inventors of new ideas for which there is a dire need in Canada.
Before sitting down I want to say that Canada is so far behind in education, as shown in the development of new technologies, that we do not have the choice of waiting to develop our own technology. We must buy technology from overseas and license it in Canada to get the country moving. This is a direct result of the lack of sufficient funds in the post-secondary educational stream. In order to turn around the economy and get it growing again, tax incentives must be put in place so that parents from the time their children are born receive tax deductions for saving money to educate the children and/or themselves. I plead with the Government to reconsider this. If it does not, I can promise that the next Government, which will be formed by the Progressive Conservative Party, will address this problem. We are aware that it is a critical problem. We hear words from different Members opposite, but we do not see any action. Through the polls, the Canadian public has told them very clearly that they are sick of their inaction and ready for a change of government. No matter who they put in charge, they still want us to take over, manage and run the economy in a proper way.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977. When we observe the way the Government and the Minister have handled both education and health in terms of dealing with the problem, we see that the Government brings forward programs without enough negotiation with the provinces. In other words, they promote a political program, put it forward and then tell the provinces to pay for it.
In the area of health, our Party is dedicated to the universal medicare program. We believe it should be given high priority. However, this should be done through negotiation with the provinces. We should tell the provinces what it will cost, what will be the program and arrive at arrangements regarding the cost-shared programs. What do we have ? The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) takes a certain direction for political expediency and dumps it on the provinces. That is very unfair.
In terms of education, I have been particularly concerned about on-the-job training. There are steps the Government could take to strengthen the Canadian position and prepare people to pick up education on the job. This would strengthen our economy.
I want to deal with small businesses and farming in relation to education. How do we prepare our young people to take on these jobs? There is no educational program in the case of small business. Our young people receive book training. We send them to school for a number of years. However, we then throw them into the job market. They are not prepared to meet that challenge.
I have seen this happen in the construction business for years. There should be training programs for the various trades such as carpentry or construction in general. Are we
April 12, 1984

preparing our young people? Do we have proper training programs to educate our young people to go out on a job? This is one area that the Government should take a close look at, and not only in terms of construction.
Let us take a look at the rural areas. One problem in this country is that we have become too centralized. We have had a program of centralization. The Liberal Government has poured too much into the large centres and this has created problems. We should now look at decentralization, possibly even in terms of education and preparing people for jobs. People must go where the jobs are. I will use a homely example. You may need someone to operate a tractor. If you want to hire a young person, you run into a number of government regulations, both provincial and federal. These regulations would, in fact, even preclude what I would call on-the-job training so that a person would be able to operate a machine in a proper way. This, of course, requires direct input from the person who operates the small business or farm so that that kind of an education program can be extended. The Government has done nothing to extend training in a practical way.
Unless we get down to a practical base at both the provincial and federal levels, we will not solve our problems. I think one of today's most overrated phrases is "high technology". There should certainly be emphasis on high-tech education, but I would like to express my opinion about this subject, Mr. Speaker. I do not presume to be an expert in the area of high technology but I have seen things work in a practical way in the small business and agricultural sectors and even on the assembly lines. It is my opinion that high technology will not solve all of the problems. We must become very practical and find out where the jobs are and where the productivity is. This will mean that our educational system will have to offer massive retraining programs, yet I believe that the system has not even begun to explore the various practical ideas and solutions that governments could implement.
Through the years, I have had the opportunity to employ many young students who were perhaps 16 or 17 years of age and were brought up in a small town. These students had no experience of operating construction or agricultural machines. Teaching these students takes a great deal of patience and costs a lot of money. Teaching a student to use a piece of equipment which costs $100,000 requires a great deal of responsibility. Someone must tutor a student by showing him how to check the oil in the morning and how to operate the machine in a variety of circumstances. If the Government were to offer tax benefits to operators in the construction and agricultural sectors to teach students, we could create some employment. I have heard of cases of young people who, because they were not working, got into trouble with the law. I think this is one area in which the Government can act in terms of practical education which will put people to work.
I shall now turn to the part of the Bill which deals with health. I think it is most unfair that the Government has used
Established Programs Financing the issue of health for political expedience. It has become evident in the last few months that the Government has been mining for favourable subjects to use because the Government in front of us is bankrupt. It is most unfair of the Government to use the issue of health as a political issue. Health care is something to which we are all entitled.
It is unfair that the Government, instead od dealing with the provinces in a businesslike way and with the best interests of the Canadian people at heart, has used the issue of health as a political tool. I think that is very, very wrong, Mr. Speaker. If we are to have a country which is united in its strengths, we must remove from the political spectrum the type of thing we have seen demonstrated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Ministers responsible for health in the various provinces feel very strongly about the misuse of this type of issue. They feel very strongly about the fact that the Government has indicated that it is the only entity in Canada which is interested in the health and welfare of the Canadian people. We on this side of the House are certainly dedicated to the health, education and welfare of the Canadian people.
Per capita transfers to post-secondary education will escalate quite significantly. It will become important to look at the future and implement a program to address the problem of education. We must redirect people from one area of education to another area of employment. This is probably one of the greatest problems the country will face. Young people who spend many years educating themselves in their desired professions find out that the whole system has collapsed on them. One of the greatest problems facing young people in the days ahead will be that, after having chosen a profession and educating themselves in that profession and having spent time, money and effort, they find that there are no jobs. This Government or the next Conservative Government must face that great challenge.
We must explore the areas of high technology but that is not where the answer lies. High technology may answer the problems of a few people but it will also create some problems. We must explore the area of practical training so that our young people do not find themselves in the chaotic situation which exists today.
The unemployment rate is the highest it has been in the history of the country. I heard this morning that in the maritime provinces the unemployment rate is staggeringly high, as high as 30 per cent. This should not be happening in a country with such vast opportunities and so many natural resources. Canadians could be accused of over-emphasizing the natural resources of this great country. However, I think that when preparing our young people for the challenge ahead, we have missed the point and are not redirecting Canadians so that they may do the things which they do the best.
Without zeroing in on a great deal of expenditure and bad mismanagement on behalf of Canadians, we have seen some good examples of this in recent days. I believe the Minister responsible for education on the government side should be

April 12, 1984
Established Programs Financing reconsidering this program and asking himself whether Canadians are being directed toward areas that will stimulate the country, productivity and ensure jobs for young people in the future. We need a new program for the redirection of funds and efforts so that young people are not trained or retrained in fields in which they will not be able to find a job.
Some may say that it is unfair to address this issue in those hard terms, but I suggest it is the Government's responsibility to be the vehicle for opening doors so that the private sector and the Government can study areas where this can be accomplished. We cannot accomplish the goals we set for this country when governments get caught up in political bickering.
When I consider the tremendous potential of this country, I cannot help but think of the situation in western Canada with regard to the National Energy Program. I have seen thousands of jobs lost when the markets of the world were there for us. The House will recall the period when we were importing oil from Mexico and losing jobs. Oil rigs were shut down and I believe as many as 275 went across the line. This meant the loss of thousands of jobs for our young people and thousands of dollars to our treasuries. As well, it cost us in terms of welfare payments. It was a terrible loss to the country and one from which we have not begun to recover at this point.
There must be long-term planning with a view to providing what we are asking of our young people. Is the Government asking them to go without jobs, to be ill-prepared and continue in technologies which we have not been prepared to deal with through our educational system? Furthermore, when government mismanagement is added to this, it results in a very serious situation. I suggest that it is important to look at this whole area of retraining and fiscal responsibility as it relates to the balance of payments between provincial and federal governments so that we can give young people the opportunity to prepare themselves and assure their future with stable jobs. This can be accomplished in this country with good management.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill C-12 which relates to federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, having particular application to both secondary education and health, is drawing to a close. For that reason, I believe it is important to highlight some of the major features of Bill C-12 as it affects the legislative base for the federal-provincial arrangements that, in turn, govern the delivery of post-secondary education services and health services right across Canada.
First and foremost, we must recognize that federal-provincial relations have evolved over a long period of time. In more recent decades, federal-provincial relations have been formalized to a great extent with the result that the federal-provincial conference has become a kind of institution. In the last few years the process of institutionalizing federal-provincial relations has fallen into difficult straits. On several occasions, we
have read in newspapers and other forms of media publications that federal-provincial relations are dying, that co-operative federalism is dead. That presents difficulties for governments at federal, provincial and indeed municipal levels. If there is one thing that is essential to the welfare of this country and the governing of all parts and aspects of our national life, it is co-operation among the various levels of government, particularly the federal and provincial governments.
In that context it is important to review Bill C-12 and its effect on post-secondary education and health programs across Canada. In order to illustrate my point, I would refer to a report published by the provincial Ministers of Finance in April of 1983. It is made very clear in that report that, in the opinion of the provincial Ministers, there are great and grave difficulties with the federal Government's policies with respect to the funding of post-secondary education and health.
One point made in that report is that the federal proposals with respect to funding bear no relationship to actual provincial spending on health and higher education. I suggest that the importance of that point escapes many Members of the House of Commons and possibly other Canadians. It is a terrible reflection on the policies of the federal Government when provincial Ministers say in a formal report that its policies with respect to funding of the important area of post-secondary education and health are not related to what is actually taking place in those fields and that the funding of education and health is an academic exercise, a national operation that bears no relationship to what is actually happening.
As a result, health and education expenses in the provinces can go up in order to meet the needs and challenges of people of each of the provinces, while the federal participation, in effect, can go down. That points out very clearly and concisely what the problem is. It is that the Government of Canada, in dealing with the important subjects of health and education, has escaped from reality into formulas that may protect the federal Treasury but do not provide the services which all Canadians have agreed must be provided.
The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) mentioned in his speech earlier today that the federal Government takes advantage of the fact that the province is responsible for actually providing services in health and education so that any failure to provide an adequate service reflects immediately on the provincial government and officers while not affecting, in an immediate way, the Government and officers of Canada. That creates a very difficult situation because if the Government of Canada takes advantage of that type of insulation from the people of Canada in the important areas of health and education and in effect tries to deceive the people of Canada with respect to the role that the federal Government plays in these matters, it will undermine the confidence of Canadians not only in the federal Government but in government at all levels.
One might suspect my motives in making that statement, but in fact even more extreme statements have been made by responsible persons, such as the President of the Canadian
April 12, 1984

Medical Association. In fact, I have a publication here dated March 20, 1984, in which the President of the Canadian Medical Association said this, and I quote:
The President of the Canadian Medical Association today accused the Minister of National Health and Welfare and members of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs of perpetrating political fraud against the Canadian public.
When you put together the statement contained in the report of the provincial Ministers of Finance and the statement published by the Canadian Medical Association accusing the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) of political fraud against the Canadian public, you realize the state of federal-provincial relations and what a disastrous effect that must have on very important fields like health and higher education. I believe that is an important observation and one which should concern all Canadians with respect to Bill C-12 and its effect on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, which in turn determine the services which will be provided in the fields of health and higher education. Health and education become the victims of difficulties in federal-provincial relations.
The death of co-operative federalism takes its toll in those important service areas of health and education. I believe it is a sad day for the House of Commons and for all Canadians when, as a result of the failure of the federal Government to deal properly with the provincial governments, those needed services in health and education suffer.
The pith and substance of this Bill and related legislation is that, in fact, it reduces the funding available to post-secondary educational institutions and to the deliverers of health services in Canada. One can present many statistics but the bottom line is that there will be less money available. When you are talking, Mr. Speaker, of education cost across Canada, you are talking of a total expenditure of $4.7 billion. Governments provide almost 72 per cent, 73 per cent of that amount, approximately $3.4 billion. The balance of the funds, which amounts to less than 27 per cent, 28 per cent, comes from the private sector and tuition fees. Therefore, if the federal Government reduces the amount it is willing to spend in the field of post-secondary education, it does not take much calculation to realize that the bottom line is increased tuition fees to the students of Canada to the extent that the private sector cannot make up the shortage of funds. Any dramatic increase in tuition fees of Canadian universities and post-secondary institutions immediately affects the accessibility of young Canadians to higher education. If there is one objective which most Canadians have, it is to acquire a higher education, if their abilities and capacities permit them to absorb that level of training and education.
We cannot divorce the problem from the realities of life. When we reduce the amount of federal funding to post-secondary education, it not only leads to reduced services at the universities, but affects in a very real way the accessibility of young Canadians to a university level education. I want to point out again, as I have in the past, the realities of this
Established Programs Financing
legislative measure as it affects Canadian university students. We are not talking about a small number of Canadians, Mr. Speaker. There are over 500,000 young Canadians enrolled in post-secondary institutions on a full-time or part-time basis. In addition, there are many more persons who are, in effect, students at Canadian universities and post-secondary institutions pursuing subjects of instruction which will not result in a university degree, but which, nonetheless, allows them to participate in the process of secondary education.
Finally, I would like to express my concern for Canadian university students by pointing out that in 1982-1983 there was a 15.9 per cent increase in tuition fees across Canada. With measures like those contained in Bill C-12, that increase is liable to escalate dramatically in the next years. The importance, I should note, of that average 15.9 per cent increase across Canada is that in some provinces it is quite extreme. In the Province of Newfoundland, the increase in tuition fees for 1982-1983 is estimated to be 37.1 per cent. Provinces which have delayed increasing tuition fees can expect even greater increases in the next time period. It is anticipated in the Province of British Columbia, for example, that tuition fees at the University of British Columbia could increasee by 33 per cent or more in the next few years.
We have a real, practical problem, Mr. Speaker. We are not talking in abstract about a cold and sterile process of government funding. We are talking about the ability of young Canadians to have access to higher education. We are talking about the level of the services provided to students at universities and post-secondary institutions, and other things of a very practical nature.
There are many other concerns, Mr. Speaker, in the educational field which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. However, I would like to deal now with the other part of Bill C-12 which affects the health field. In addition to Bill C-12, we have before us in this House Bill C-3 which enacts the new Canada Health Act. We know what difficulties that Bill has created for the health professions across Canada and for other persons and institutions involved in the delivery of health care services. I have already mentioned the accusation of political fraud which has been made by the Canadian Medical Association, but again we have the practical effect of a reduction in financing on the services provided by those persons and institutions who depend upon that government financing.
Provinces like the Province of Nova Scotia already expend over 25 per cent of their revenue dollars on health. It simply has no more funds to apply to health care services. I believe that is true of most provinces in Canada as we approach this lower level in the economic recession cycle. The unfortunate part, Mr. Speaker, is that it is very unlikely that the situation will improve even with an improvement in the economy, because all we can do in the next decade is reach the status we have enjoyed in past decades. There is very little opportunity and chance totally to revitalize the economy in such a way that funds will be generated from normal taxation sources to make up the deficits which have accrued, not only in the total

April 12, 1984
Established Programs Financing
national revenue picture, but in all the services which are involved in that picture, and health services, including medical care, is one of those services.
What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that it is unlikely that anything will happen in the next year by way of economic improvement which will generate any great amount of funds for a service like health care. We must, therefore, rely on the standard sources of funds. We must rely on the standard programs which have been provided to support health care.
This Bill, Mr. Speaker, is another example of reducing in a very insidious way the amount of funds which will actually flow through to the deliverers of health care services. Yet, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding that reduction in funding available for health care, the Government pretends and purports to be improving health care in Canada. The Government purports to be helping Canadians in relation to health care. There should be little wonder that the Canadian Medical Association has accused the Minister of National Health and Welfare of political fraud.
One always likes to be positive, particularly when the subject is post-secondary education and health. However, there is an element of fraud in what the Government has been doing in the legislative field as represented by Bill C-12 and by other Bills in the House. There is ample evidence that a fraud is being perpetrated on the Canadian people. At the very time that the Government is withdrawing funds from important areas like health and education, it is pretending to assist and advance the services provided in those important fields.
The debate on Bill C-12 is drawing to an end. It may well be that my remarks will terminate the debate on third reading. I believe it is very unfortunate that as we terminate that debate it is on the note that not only are there difficulties now in the fields of health and higher education, but that those who are involved in those very important fields can look forward in the next few years to even greater difficulties. This lack of funding will have its effect on those who will now be required to pay for the services. In the case of post-secondary education it will be the students, in the case of health services it will be the provincial Governments, the alternative being a reduction in service. Either way it is going to be difficult for the people of Canada.

Just a short question. From watching the Conservatives perform in debate on this legislation and on the health Bill, it would appear that they are talking out of both sides of their mouth. They advocate support of, but vote
against, in some cases, provisions which would improve postsecondary education.
I notice that most of their speakers failed to touch adequately on native education. The Hon. Member talks about the Government committing a fraud on the Canadian people. I wonder why we have not heard anything from the Official Opposition on this subject, which is clearly a federal responsibility. We should be insisting that provinces make an adequate contribution to the post-secondary education of native people. There should be a high spending priority on university education and technical and vocational training programs which could be funded at the post-secondary level. Mr. Speaker, I recently had the opportunity to bring to the attention of the House of Commons the seriousness of driving while impaired. Mr. Speaker, I never fail to be amazed by the extravagance of the Government. Mr. Speaker, the Ontario Supreme Court recently reversed a lower court decision in the Medhurst case and ruled that the father of an unborn child has no legal status to prevent the unborn child from being aborted.
The Supreme Court based its decision on previous court rulings which have declared that an unborn child is not a person. The decision thereby prohibits a father from acting legally as a "next friend" of the fetus which he and his wife created.
While the Criminal Code allows for abortions if an abortion committee in an accredited hospital finds that the woman's life or health would be endangered by the pregnancy or birth, the judge in the Medhurst case stated that even if there were reason to believe the abortion committee had not fulfilled its legal requirements, it would still not be for him or any other judge to decide whether or not a woman should have an abortion.
In light of the Medhurst case, and the undisputed scientific proof set out in the Borowski case in which Judge Matheson of the Queen's Bench of Saskatchewan acknowledged beyond question that a fetus is a human being, I urge the Government to initiate action under the amending formula to amend the Constitution so that the human fetus will be included under the protective provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, as has already been done in West Germany.

subtopic: PETROLEUM AND GAS REVENUE TAX ACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacLaren that Bill C-14, an Act to amend an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: PETROLEUM AND GAS REVENUE TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to join in the debate on Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas. This is basically an Act to amend the PGRT, which has become very famous initials, and to put in line with a number of other Acts a number of definitions that had been placed in the previous Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act and the Income Tax Act.
This Act is also intended to give credibility to some of the Budget provisions that have been in place for a number of years now for which the legislation has never been passed. It is astonishing that Budgets can pass this House and on the evening of the Budget taxes are in place and being collected by the Government. Yet the Government does not move with any speed legitimately to pass the legislation in the House that gives the tax some effect. This is the case with this legislation.
The $250,000 tax credit has been in place. It allows for a corporation to have an annual credit of up to $250,000. That liability can be deducted from the petroleum and gas revenue tax. It has been in effect since it was announced in the NEP update. It is basically a good measure. This allows a company some cash flow and allows it to make further decisions, hopefully to drill in the Canadian basin.
We also have a reduction in royalties. This is another tax relief measure. We have royalty reduction from 16 per cent to 14.67 per cent, which really is a reduction from the exact rate of 12 per cent to 11 per cent. That was effective from June 1, 1982 to May 31, 1983. It has also been announced in the NEP update. This measure is being provided for in the Bill yet in effect it has already lapsed. This Bill is giving legitimacy to the Budget which put forward this reduction in royalties. A Bill has never been passed to give that royalty reduction any legitimacy. It could be argued that although the measure is no longer in effect it still allows corporations legally to file for that reduction.
In the April 19, 1983 Budget there was also introduced and placed in this Act an enhanced oil recovery program. It basically provided for a reduction from income of capital costs in enhanced oil recovery projects. The damage of the national program was already in place. Companies such as Dome and Imperial Oil had projects in place in Judy Creek. There are still large amounts of oil in the ground but it cannot be brought out of the ground by conventional pumping methods. A series of expensive measures must be used to bring this oil to
Elisabeth Nadeau Martin Boulianne Brian Kelly Claude Lussier Lise Tremblay Reine Villeneuve Martin Cauchon Diane Gagnon

April 12, 1984
Petroleum and Gas
the surface. Some incentive is required for companies to take on such a project. Many projects which had been envisioned by companies were cancelled when the National Energy Program came in. They did not have the cash flow any more to go forward with these projects.
I can remember an exciting project just west of my home. When carbon dioxide is pumped into a well it provides what many of the people who work in the area call the "milk shake effect". It stirs up the oil in the ground, takes it out of the pores of the rocks and allows it to be pumped to the surface. The proposal that was put forward was to use the carbon dioxide from the coal-fired electrical plant for this process. That carbon dioxide was going into the atmosphere as waste. It could be used with no production cost. It could, in effect, give life to that field. Of course, that project was cancelled with the National Energy Program. Now we have a Bill that is attempting to bring some more life into the enhanced oil recovery program.
If we look at the statistics, we will find that much of the western oil basin that has been producing oil since 1948 basically-some wells in the Turner Valley area before that, but the major discovery was after 1948-has been declining at a rate of about 30,000 barrels per day per year. The statistics do not show that because we have brought on stream two tar sands plants. In the last few years since coming on stream they have produced a substantial amount of oil, which shows increased production from the western oil basin. In effect, our oil production from coventional crude oil was, in 1982, 16 per cent less than in 1979, and it is feasible to believe that unless we find more oil in these basins that could decrease by as much as 10 per cent per year in the future.
Part of the reason we are not adding to that western oil basin or supply is that since the National Energy Program far fewer wells are being drilled searching for oil. In the last few months there have been some interesting discoveries in northern Alberta. There has been some substantial drilling going on in the Saskatchewan basin.
Why is it that we have more drilling in the Saskatchewan area? It is not because of anything the federal Government has done. The National Energy Program is still in place. The PRGT is still in place. But the Saskatchewan Government has allowed oil companies that find oil a royalty holiday of up to five years on these new wells. You might ask why they would forgo that kind of income. It is logical to say that if there are no wells drilled, there are no jobs, no trucks are bought, no people are working and there is nothing to tax. It is far better to allow companies that are prepared to take this kind of financial risk a royalty holiday so they can provide employment to the local citizens in the area. And if there is a possibility of finding oil they can quickly recover their costs.
When you consider that wells in the western basin cost upwards of $500,000 per hole at this time, you can understand that the companies do not want that money sitting for very long. What does this do? Perhaps this is something we should
consider applying in other areas, and the federal Government ought to take some leadership in this regard. As this Bill is reducing the PGRT in certain instances, perhaps we might make the suggestion that for new wells drilled in Saskatchewan, Alberta-in any part of the nation-the federal Government forgo any portion of the taxes it levies on the oil industry, and that the provincial governments match the amount in royalty. We then have to get the industry moving again.
What would this do? This would move us more quickly to self-sufficiency. One of the objects of the National Energy Program that has not come about is a move toward self-sufficiency. By removing billions of dollars from existing oil production, mainly in western Canada, and placing that money through the PIP grants into the so-called Canada Lands in the North and in the offshore in the main, we have not been as fortunate as many who proposed the program thought we would be. We have not found energy that could quickly be brought on stream in the Northwest Territories, in the Beaufort, and in the eastern offshore.
However, there is a plus side. This has brought forward the potential of about 1.5 billion barrels of oil in Hibernia. This most likely will not come on stream for up to six to ten years. The Beaufort Sea still has promise, but there has been no development of a commercial reservoir yet. Part of the reason, I believe, is that the petroleum incentive grants have been on the exploratory side and not in the production area. What the companies are tending to do is drill wells to find the extension of the field, rather than delineate the field for actual production. In other words, to detemine the extent of the field where they have drilled and found oil, and whether the field can produce. We are spending billions of dollars in incentives and yet we are getting very little in the sense that there might be some production in the near future.
When a well is drilled in the western Canadian basin and oil is found, the potential to bring that oil on stream very quickly is excellent. That could quickly add to our self-sufficiency needs. What would be more in the interests of our nation is to get some equity in the system so that both could take place, and in that was we could again encourage drilling so that oil can be found in the western basin with thousands of jobs being provided.
One of the negative aspects of the National Energy Program is the taking of money out of the western basin and putting it into the off-shore, because it costs $100 million a well to drill in the off-shore, whereas the cost is approximately $500,00 a well in the Western basin. Both require approximately the same number of men to perform the duty. It is no wonder that since the National Energy Program was brought into existence we have lost about 40 per cent of the jobs in that industry in the Western part of Canada. This translates into anywhere from 20,000 to 40,000 jobs. Those jobs could be quickly brought back on stream if we brought some order into this taxation system and the grants as they are now in place.
Another difficulty with the PGRT, the up-front taxation of oil, as it comes from the well, and natural gas, is in the area of the petrochemical industry. We have in my constituency two
April 12, 1984

large world-scale plants. One of those plants provides all the basic stock for the total industry of Canada. Within the nation we have a number of these large world-scale petrochemical plants. We have them in Sarnia, Montreal, and there are two in the Edmonton region. They are required to move their product into the international market. They have been doing very well at that until recently. We now find that their competitive edge, because oil prices and natural gas prices have not gone as high as predicted, is being lost to the gulf region of the United States, to Mexico-which is bringing on a petrochemical industry-and to Saudi Arabia, a large petrochemical region. They are not charging upfront taxes. In fact, feedstock going into those petrochemical industries is basically going in at the country's cost.
Given our advantages and given the need to find and hold on to new markets before our competitors are in place, we must quickly react to the proposals of the petrochemical industry task force which indicated that there ought to be a market-responsive price for the feedstock going into that industry. This means that rather than taxing the product as it flows into the petrochemical plant, taxation by the Government ought to be on the product as it flows out and into world markets.
The task force also indicated that if there was no tax we ought not to be concerned because we have in place thousands of people who are working. If we do not get the system in place very quickly, the add-ons to the Prentiss and Joffre plants in my constituency will not take place and the people there in the construction industry will lose their jobs. Are we prepared to accept that so the Government can continue to collect the upfront taxation on the feedstock going into those areas? Would it not be better to have the jobs in place and the markets found, anticipating that perhaps in the future there might be profits of which government could take advantage and tax. That makes more sense to me.
It is important as will to look at the many definitions in the Bill. One has to be somewhat of an expert-and we have a few in this Party-to understand a production royalty versus a resource royalty. There is an attempt in the legislation to extract the proper definitions. This is important for companies that are looking to find the most available tax system under which to operate. There are some proposals in the Bill which deal with the definition of royalties.
This Bill will not in any way assist the very serious problems resulting from the National Energy Program. It provides some things which are attractive to the industry, but it does not deal with the lack of drilling in the western sedimentary basin, with the lack of proper tax incentives to get an upgrader in the heavy oil areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta, or with the jobs and oil available from the tar sands which we know can be onstream in a number of years.
