speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in that part of this great country from which I come we saw water power being used to turn the wheels of machinery, only to have those water courses diverted into hydraulic raceways to supply yet another form of economic energy. Our earlier generations harnessed the great Niagara to provide electrical energy in an economically expansive manner. Energy as we saw it then and the cost of energy were matters of concern to those people who lived in that area a long time ago. We knew then that Canada's energy resources could be, and still can be the engine of growth that this country so badly needs.
We in Niagara remember well the 1980 election. That was the election in which the Liberal Party talked in terms of 18 cents at the gas pumps. They hoodwinked the people with respect to the cost of energy: "Tell the public that what the Conservatives are proposing to do is nothing less than usury, but for goodness sake don't tell them the truth about the cost of energy production and, for goodness sake, don't tell them what we as a party in power or in government would do with respect to the cost of producing energy."
It took the present Government less than one year to raise the cost of that energy production in excess of 18 cents at the gas pump which it was so quick to deny and denounce during the 1980 election campaign. Gasoline prices today, of course, bear no relationship whatsoever to that which was suggested in the fall of 1979 or early months of 1980. If the voters in 1980 had known what they know now, if they had known that $2 a gallon for gasoline in 1984 would be a bargain rate, the election result might have been different. The Government across the way might have been faced with a lesser degree of credibility.
Might I suggest that the voting public soon began to realize the lengths that the Party in Government would go to keep power. For them, history has shown that power does corrupt. This is why I am disappointed with the legislation before us today.
There is no visionary outlook in Bill C-16. This Bill offers nothing new to what was announced earlier, first in the National Energy Program update in June, 1982 and in the Budget of last April. Canadians looking for relief from soaring energy costs will find no comfort in this legislation. Even worse, this legislation fails to put energy mega projects such as the tar sands or any other imaginative program back on track so that energy can be the engine of economic Canadian growth. It lacks the vision of working thousands. It lacks the vision of the wheels turning and the building of pride and confidence in being Canadian. Instead, Parliament's time is being devoted to a rather technical Bill, almost of a housekeeping nature, sanctioning past Cabinet decisions. The opportunity is gone. The opportunity to address the problems which all Canadians know exist under the National Energy Program is being thrown away.
No one, and least of all this Party, can have any reservations about supporting the goals and ideal principles of the National Energy Program. Canadianization, security of supply and energy self-sufficiency are all endorsed by us. If the House will forgive me, they are motherhood issues. We like them. However, the comment cannot be said of the means by which this Government has chosen to reach these goals.
In its self-righteousness, the Government has created a monster Petro-Canada, destroyed the energy megaprojects, has driven record numbers of oil rigs to the United States and elsewhere and has sent energy prices soaring in all spheres of activity. Bill C-14 does not address the serious deficiencies of the National Energy Program. Indeed, legislation has not even been introduced to address one of the most contentious aspects
April 12, 1984

of the National Energy Program, the Canadian ownership charge.
This charge was introduced to pay for the acquisition of Petrofina by Petro-Canada. Petrofina has long since been paid for, yet Canadians go on paying the ownership charge every time they purchase a litre or gallon of gasoline. We question again the morality of this Government and the integrity of that Party which fixes a 4.5 cents a gallon charge for the clearly specified purpose of purchasing Petrofina and then continuing to gather from the consumers of this country $800 million a year, long after the Canadians people paid the cost, excessive as it was, of Petrofina.
It is not too cynical of me to suggest that the only necessity for the continuation of that charge is this Government's continuing appetite for spending; for example, purchasing ridings at the rate of $500,000. In my view, Canadian consumers would do a much better job of efficiently spending and effectively getting a return from the $800 million a year charged to them through this ownership charge.
Even though the Canadian ownership charge is bad, Canadians should not be allowed to forget that it would have been worse had it not been for the bell ringing episode of March, 1982. Buried in that mammoth energy legislation introduced as Bill C-94 was a proposal to allow for the raising of this charge, not to 4.6 cents per gallon but to 16 cents per gallon. Had the legislation been allowed to stand as it was, and had this cash-starved Government raised those charges as it had earlier proposed, Canadians would be losing over $3 billion a year. We on this side of the House stopped that increase dead in its tracks. However, we could have done so earlier with the full support of Canadians across the country.
Canadian people knew perfectly well by that time the worth of the Government's promise or commitment. They had seen its actions and had been deceived by the Government through the National Energy Program. Then as now, we demanded that changes be made to the National Energy Program. Bill C-14 is but one small part of what needs to be done.
As the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. Mulroney) pointed out in Calgary last November, energy policy in the country must once more reflect a sense of realism. The fanciful dreams of bureaucrats and Cabinet Ministers have caused enough damage already. It is self-evident that the sense of realism most needed is an acceptance of the fact that the National Energy Program cannot operate in a vacuum. For example, unrealistic revenue forecasts led to the creation of a Petroleum Incentives Program. Those revenues did not materialize, but the program continues nevertheless. The program continues to the extent that the Auditor General, when looking at the number of grants made, was moved to ask where the returns are.
Many complaints can be levelled against this program. My complaint and the complaint of anyone with a modicum of concern for the Canadian shipbuilding industry is about its negative impact on that industry alone. To put it into perspec-
Petroleum and Gas
tive, Mr. Speaker, the House should consider that the private sector once accounted for over 80 per cent of the work done in Canadian shipyards. The private sector today accounts for less than 20 per cent in tonnage terms of the work done in those same shipyards.
While there may be many reasons for this reversal, the petroleum incentive grant is a major factor and I will tell you why this is so. A Canadian company leasing foreign-built offshore oil rigs is eligible for grants to cover 80 per cent of those leasing costs. If a company decides to buy a foreign-built offshore oil rig, the company can recover up to 80 per cent of the duty paid. However, a company buying a Canadian-built rig for offshore drilling is not eligible for the grants at all. This is the Government's greatest lesson in a give-and-take program.
Not surprisingly, then, Mr. Speaker, most of the offshore rigs operating off the East Coast or in the Beaufort Sea are foreign built. Not surprisingly then, our shipyards are looking for work. In St. Catharines, the Port Weller Shipyards are working at less than 30 per cent capacity with less than 30 per cent employment.
The program clearly needs adjustment on a priority basis. Yet today we are discussing Bill C-14, part of which gives legislative blessing to a measure which has already been adopted and, in part, even lapsed. I would have thought that the shipbuilding industry warranted greater consideration than that.
Others in the House, particularly those of us on this side, have discussed at some considerable length the technical aspects of this legislation. I do not propose to review that ground. However, other Hon. Members have pointed out how perplexing it is that this Bill should precede Parliament's consideration of matters of pressing concern in the energy sector.
Why should the cost of our energy needs at the gas pump, in our homes or elsewhere be so much higher in this country than the cost to consumers in the United States of America? Where is the justification for continuing the expropriation charge made in the name of a Canadian window on the industry? These issues along with the Petroleum Incentives Program have been pushed aside by Bill C-14. This is a reflection of the depths to which the National Energy Program has fallen. The Government has clearly lost any sense of direction and Bill C-14 is further evidence of that. The Bill will never even begin to restore its direction.

I suggest this demonstrates the policies of trial and error of the Government. With that kind of approach to the management of the most important affairs in our country, we have a situation in which the Government first, through its policies of trial and error, destroys and then attemps to restore. In this case we are dealing with a classic example of a very basic and
Petroleum and Gas
fundamental policy failure. This kind of government mentality and philosophy in the National Energy Program has destroyed one of the most viable industries in the country and one of the major engines of growth. It was one of the major job creators which, in many respects, was distinctively Canadian, at least at the exploration and service level. The Canadian content and participation in terms of the number of jobs was a very major component to this industry.
It causes one to look at other policies which follow this same philosophy of trial and error; destroy and restore. Look at what the Government is doing in the case of VIA Rail passenger service-clearly the same thing. It unilaterally, without any consideration for the public, without any public input or reference to parliamentary debate, dismantled 20 per cent of Canada's rail passenger service in this country.

He was out in Jasper last weekend and talked about the need of restoring the rail passenger service between Vancouver and Edmonton. He said if it was going to be restored it was going to have to be a joint funding arrangement with the three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal. Does that mean there is a complete new policy with respect to the rail passenger service in this country? Or is it just simply a policy for the west? However, that is merely a side issue, Mr. Speaker. The fact of the matter is that this Government sought in 1981 to destroy the rail passenger system in this country and now it is attempting to put it back together.

Yes, I am talking from experience, you bet. I remember some of the things they used to do in those days, Mr. Speaker, especially the used car operators. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, when the Chrysler Corporation-and this is not a plug for Chrysler because I was not a Chrysler dealer-came out with a very attractive warranty. It was called five years or 50,000 miles, whichever occurs first. Some of these used car fly-by-nighters used to set up their business and a customer would come in to buy a car and ask what the warranty was. They would be told it was five and five. When asked what it stood for, the dealer would say "five miles or five minutes, whichever occurs first". But if the customer did not ask the question, he would have gone out thinking he was getting something more than he really was. If he did not ask, he would assume it had some meaning.
That was exactly what happened with the National Energy Program, Mr. Speaker, quite frankly. Canadians really thought they were going to get a fair break in terms of price. They thought they were going to be treated fairly. They thought there was going to be some opportunity to invest. They thought there was going to be some opportunity to expand the energy sector in this country rather than have it contracted. The fact of the matter is that those things did not occur. That policy of trial and error did a great disservice to the energy sector of this country, particularly the fossil fuel sector.
It is really interesting, Mr. Speaker, to remember that this National Energy Program was to have helped Canadian companies, but the Canadian companies which really got drawn into the finite elements of the National Energy Program are the ones which find themselves in the most difficulty, Dome Petroleum, Sulpetrol, Turbo, all because they were lured into making huge investments and undertakings on the basis of the National Energy Program. What is more tragic, Mr. Speaker, is that a very vibrant and vital service industry, the service and exploration industry, which is a very vital component of the energy sector, was literally gutted and dismantled, and with it hundreds upon hundreds of small business enterprises went down the tube. Many of these small businesses were family enterprises. Many of them started with the boom of the oil industry, going back to the 1950s.
What we are doing now, Mr. Speaker, in the process of this Bill, is attempting to repair and restore some semblance of fairness and equity into the policies which affect the development of energy. We hear a lot of things from Liberal leadership candidates these days about the National Energy Program. Some support it and some do not, which is rather strange. The Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston) does not like the National Energy Program. 1 take it that the honourable John Turner does not like the National Energy Program. It is amazing how those boys were silent when the National Energy Program was delivering such a crushing blow to that very vital industry. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) was in Edmonton two or three weeks ago talking to the Liberal Party faithful. He stated that Alberta should welcome the collapse of the boom because the megaprojects were too big,
too difficult to manage, too difficult to finance and too risky. What he is really saying is, "Well, boys, you are really lucky that the National Energy Program came along because we saved you from the boom, from the fact that these megaprojects were going to be too difficult to manage, and were going to overheat the economy". What he is really saying, Mr. Speaker, is that the people of Alberta should thank him for the 14 per cent level of unemployment, for the crashing real estate market, for the bankruptcies and the broken dreams, hopes and aspirations of so many who went down the tube.
The national energy policy, as far as most people in Alberta are concerned, was the most odious policy ever perpetrated upon one single region. Quite frankly, I think it was more than simply a policy of trial and error. I think it was a deliberate plot to destroy one of the very main engines of economic activity in Canada. But I give thanks for the intelligence of Canadians. The people right across the country recognized, long before this Government, that it was unfair, it was not working and that it was affecting the central Canadian heartland. They recognized, for example, that for every dollar spent in western Canada, Ontario receives 42 cents; Quebec, 13 cents; Alberta, 29 cents, and the other provinces, 16 cents, and for every job created in the energy sector in western Canada two jobs are created somewhere else.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for suggesting that Hon. Members across the way listen attentively. I think it would do them some good, because I am not talking about the technical aspects of this Bill, I am talking about some very practical aspects, and I speak from some experience.
The Hon. Member wants to know whether I want to sell Petro-Canada. This issue does not deal with Petro-Canada. It is a going oil company owned by the people of Canada and it is in place. It has nothing to do with this legislation. If you want to bring in a bill to denationalize Petro-Canada, we will deal with it. That brings me to the issue of Canadianization.
There have been lots of statements made about Canadianization. What has happened is that there has been very little improvement in private Canadian ownership. Canadian ownership has come about largely as a result of nationalization. We are not really achieving any of the major goals enunciated when the NEP came out.
I want to make it clear that I am not arguing against the intent of this Bill. It is repairing a measure which was ill conceived at the outset. It just demonstrates how far out of line the Government was when it first initiated the NEP.
There were three principles as the major pillars of the NEP: self-suficiency, fairness and opportunity. Dealing with opportunity first, that brings into context the question of Canadianization and how well we have been doing. I put a question on the Order Paper which was answered on December 9, 1983. I asked what percentage of the petroleum industry in Canada was foreign-owned and Canadian-owned in 1980. The answer provided was that it was 73.9 per cent foreign-owned and 26.1 per cent Canadian-owned. At the end of 1982, and 1 do not have the 1983 figures because I was told that the date for 1983 is not yet available, the foreign-owned percentage was 65.8 per cent, Canadian-owned was 34.2 per cent. There has been some improvement but the key is which portion of Canadian ownership was Government owned? In 1980 it was 3.8 per cent, in 1982 it was 8.6 per cent. Private Canadian ownership was 22.3 per cent in 1980, and 25.6 per cent in 1982. So there was a measly 3 per cent increase in private Canadian ownership. So much for fulfdling the goal of Canadianization. Need I go any further on that particular point?

Let me just talk about fairness for a minute. I do not think one has to deal too long with that. Quite frankly, energy prices today are more than double what they were in 1980. The fact is that there is a great deal of price discrimination in a number of areas.
Let us talk about self-sufficiency. Quite frankly, the only thing helping us improve that is the slowdown in the economy. If you consider the heavy oil going south of the border right now, we are probably net exporters. However, we are still reliant on foreign suppliers for light and medium crude.
On this whole question of opportunity, the one I really wanted to hit on, there has been massive discrimination. Under this Government's policies and its PIP grants there has been a shift of exploration and development activity from the western sedimentary basin to the frontier and offshore. I am not arguing that that kind of exploration should not take place in some form, but it should not be shifted in total. We are the only country in the world which pays a company to drill a dry hole. We pick up 80 per cent of the tab. It cost $35 million to drill a hole in Hibernia and you could drill 120 wells in southern Alberta for that and your chances of finding oil would be a lot greater. Furthermore, to invest in the upgrading and enhancement of heavy oil would be logical way to increase our self sufficiency.
There are so many loose ends, Mr. Speaker, which need to be brought together in a cohesive and coherent energy policy that it does not seem this Government has the capacity, ability or the will to do it. I guess the only thing we will be able to do is hope and anticipate that there will be a new Government so that we can once again use energy as a major engine of economic growth to turn that natural resource into an economic opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, today we are continuing debate on Bill C-14, which is an amendment to the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act, usually referred to as the PGRT. I think what we are really discussing today is not so much the technique of how to sink an oil well or where development in the oil industry should occur, we are discussing in effect a taxation question. PGRT has a lot of impact on where development will take place, in which part of the country and could even effect different sectors of the economy.
This particular Bill chooses to deal with moneys that are collected and recycled into the petroleum industry. As I go on in my speech, I will point out where I think equal amounts of money could be used to better advantage in a period of time when the country is suffering from very high employment. I would like to spend a moment or two to set the stage and point out some of the difficulties that have arisen with regard to petroleum taxation over the past five or six years.
In 1978 of total net petroleum revenues of $8.4 billion, the federal Government received $751 million. In 1979, total revenues rose to $10.6 billion and the federal share was $797 million. In 1980, the total revenues reached $13 million from $8 billion two years before, and the federal share was $795 million. In effect the federal share of petroleum revenues had levelled out and the share of the industry and the share of the other players in the game had gone up by about $5 billion in that two-year period. The producing provinces in the petroleum industry received all of that increase. The federal Government actually lost ground in terms of the share of the

April 12, 1984
Petroleum and Gas
petroleum revenues in Canada during the 1979 to 1980 period. That was recognized by the Government in power.
When the Budget of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was read into this House in December 1979, a section appeared to recognize not only that the federal share of revenue was dropping in proportion to what it had been, but I think it recognizes very clearly that the Progressive Conservatives considered that as a principle the federal Government had the right to tax oil and gas revenues. I mention this in my speech very early, Mr. Speaker, because it is something that Members of the Official Opposition now proclaim is not the policy of the Party. But when the Conservatives were in Government, not only did they recognize that the federal Government had a share of those revenues, but in the Budget of 1979 there was a section which states, and this is from page 53 of the Budget Papers, that it is the intention of the federal Government to impose a new energy tax which would capture roughly one-half of the returns accruing from annual price increases in excess of $2 per barrel per year on oil and 30 per cent per thousand cubic feet per year on gas.
I think it was very clear in that Budget that the principle of federal rights to taxation on gas and oil was recognized by the Progressive Conservative Government of the day, and that it was prepared to increase that share.
In fact, taxation experts have calculated that that revenue would be under such a program. They estimate that between the years 1980 to 1983, which was the proposal in those Budget papers, the increase would be $7.5 billion minus whatever amounts the federal Government decided to give back by way of production incentives or tax incentives.
The policy was very clear, very well stated, and quite clearly understood, I think, by people across Canada. I only raise the matter again because sometimes it is forgotten. The question then became, how would this new tax be distributed; from where would the increases come since it had been agreed that oil prices at the wellhead would be locked into a step by step increase?
Between 1979 and 1982, the federal Government's net take from up-stream revenues increased by about $1.25 billion. They were in the neighbourhood of $795 million. During the same peak period, however, the producing provinces take rose by about $1.65 billion and the industry's share increased by $2.87 billion. The proportions of the share have changed in the ensuing years with the National Energy Program. The federal Government is now taking a larger percentage of the share, but the overall price that consumers in Canada are paying for oil and gas has increased by some 54 per cent. The Government attempted to increase the size of the pie, and at the same time increased the piece of the pie which the federal Government expected from that larger pie.
Part of what we have before us today is a decision to change the rules as they apply to the PGRT. This change covers two separate sections. I am one of the few Members of the House who was here in the late 1950s and early 1960s when the House was subjected to hundreds of divorce petitions which used to come through like sausages out of a sausage shop from the other place. divorce not only in Quebec, the odd other one came through from other regions. Ultimately Parliament did away with that by amending the Divorce Act, and Quebec accepting divorces. Let me assure the House that we wasted a great deal of time.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Bosley (Don Valley West) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the payment of municipal taxes out of after-tax income is both an unfair form of double-taxation and an impediment to home-ownership for the average Canadian; and
That the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act to permit the deduction from income, for the purposes of calculating taxable income, of all or of some maximum portion of, municipal taxes paid regarding a principal residence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have placed this motion in the narrowest possible context in order, I hope, to obtain the consent of the House for the appropriate referral. Members will not be surprised that it is my view that we need to do a great deal more than this for the encouragement and development of home ownership in the country. I believe that many of the values that have underlaid development of our society related to the ability to be secure in title to one's own property.
I could have moved a motion today that related to the deductibility of mortgage interest, that dealt with a number of issues, but that matter has been debated in an election campaign. I do not know whether it will be the subject of another election campaign. I do know that Members opposite took the position at the time that the deductability of mortgage interest
Income Tax Act
was not something they were in favour of. Therefore, today I have framed the motion in the context strictly of what I believe is an equally important matter.
Members know that every Canadian pays directly or indirectly municipal taxes, whether one is a home owner or a tenant. Every Member of this House knows, no matter what they say today as private Members if the Bill is talked out, which I hope it will not, that such a system is unfair. I want to speak briefly about the two sides of the issue. One is the unfairness of the system and the other is the need to do something to encourage home ownership for the average Canadian.
I do not think I need to say a great deal about the unfairness. Virtually everybody here knows that in order to pay $1,000 in municipal taxes today, you have to make quite a lot more than that in pre-tax income. The way our system reads, we are required to pay our municipal taxes out of our after-tax income. On its face, that is unfair. It is unfair both to home owners who have to do it directly and unfair to tenants who have to do it indirectly.
The Province of Ontario moved part way to recognize this dilemma when it brought in its property tax credit scheme. Those filing income tax returns this month in the Province of Ontario see on the form the opportunity to adjust to some degree the taxes they owe the Province of Ontario in an attempt to eliminate the double taxation system. In my view, on a straight matter of tax equity, the time to move to allow a similar deduction at the federal level is overdue. That is self evident. A great deal more does not have to be said about it.
Members of this House will recognize that there is an impediment we place through the Tax Act on the ownership of a home. I can express it as simply as this. Through tax policy, I as a taxpayer am encouraged to save for my old age by making an investment in a Registered Retirement Savings Plan. In some cases, I am encouraged to make those investments for my old age by borrowing money and in some cases the interest paid on the money borrowed is deductible from my income. However, the dream of the average Canadian is to own a home and let the home be the pension plan in the end.
In effect, Mr. Speaker, the tax policy encourages people to borrow money to do certain things but not to exercise the option of borrowing the same amount of money and putting the capital investment into a home. I believe that bias in the tax policy is one of the reasons we have increasingly become a society with a greater proportion of tenants and a smaller proportion of owners.
I represent a constituency in which 60 per cent of the residents are tenants. Not many people would expect to learn that about the riding of Don Valley West in the City of Toronto. However, that is a very normal urban phenomenon these days. A whole series of policies have led to that situation, including density encouragements for developers, land use policies of municipalities and the general attraction of cities like Toronto which bring more and more people to a relatively

April 12, 1984
Income Tax Act
confined area. As well, various levels of Government have placed impediments on the development of ownership housing.
In the simplest of terms, one of the costs a home owner must bear is his municipal taxes. Since that is a cost which is not deductible, my view is that the tax system creates a bias against a home owner. In my view, we have an obligation to correct that bias. If that were not enough, we are in effect telling people to pay one level of government tax from aftertax income and, in my view, that is an unfair system.
This matter should not be debated at great length. I believe any member of the House who does not understand this by now, after having hearing years of debate, has not been listening to the arguments on this subject. I do not believe there is a need for such arguments any longer. I would hope that Members would understand, therefore, that I have phrased this motion as narrowly as I possibly can. I believe it is time we told home owners who are struggling to maintain a home, or those who would like to be home owners but, under the current system, cannot afford to buy a home, that we believe the system is biased against their dreams and that we wish to remove that bias.
There is no suggestion in this motion that it refers to anything other than the municipal taxes on a principal residence. The motion expresses no suggestion that anyone should necessarily have the right to deduct all of their municipal taxes on all of their property. If appropriate, I am perfectly prepared to discuss with Hon. Members opposite in committee whether there should or should not be a limit on the amount of municipal taxes which may be deducted. I believe all of those questions are still open and I am perfectly prepared to have that debate. However, my personal view is that the general principle of double taxation applies no matter how large a municipal tax bill one pays. It all comes from after-tax income. I do recognize the constraints on the Treasury and I recognize the political constraints. Therefore, I have put this motion in a narrow form so that we could take one small step toward recognizing the hundreds of thousands of Canadians for whom the dream is to own a home, but cannot do so today.
If we were to begin to say to those Canadians who wish to own a home that we will begin to remove this impediment, that tax equity means we should allow municipal taxes to be deducted in whole or in part and that we will adopt the Ontario system so that tenants and home owners are treated equally, both having the right to deduct municipal taxes paid directly or indirectly, we will be taking a step in the right direction. The scheme to which I last referred would refute the argument that was advanced during the last election by some Members opposite regarding tenants' rights. In fact, most of us support the rights of tenants, and I hope it is understood that I intend this motion to apply to tenants as well as home owners.
If we could take those small steps, we would be saying that as a simple matter of principle, we want to remove the bias against home ownership from the tax system and leave the system in a more neutral position. Not only would we remove the tax bias but, in a small way, we would be stating our intentions to encourage more Canadians to attain the dream of
owning a home for themselves and their children. We would be encouraging Canadians to protect themselves against outrageous rent increases by buying a home. We would be encouraging the old Canadian tradition of saving for old age through a piece of equity which most Canadians were brought up to believe was the protection for their old age.
I offer this motion to the House in hopes that, because of its fundamental justice and because of its narrowness which eliminates the concern for those who, during the election, were worried about the breadth of this issue, I may obtain from my fellow Members of the House, in their private capacity during this hour of Private Members' Business, a recognition that action in the area of this motion is long overdue. I would therefore ask Hon. Member of the House today to allow this matter, if they possibly can, to be referred to committee for further study.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak on the motion of the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley). I must say that the proposal he has put before the House this afternoon is interesting, and in some ways appealing. Any motion which makes something deductible that is not now deductible, thus reducing federal Government income tax, is at first blush very interesting, and perhaps very appealing. However, to say that the present system is an unfair form of double taxation may not be totally accurate and could perhaps be misleading.
The Income Tax Act applies to income whereas municipal taxes are levied against property. It is wrong to suggest that the same income is being taxed twice. Through municipal taxes, we are paying for certain services provided by the municipality, just as we pay for any essential goods and services provided by the private sector. Those private sector costs are paid with after-tax dollars. Does that mean that they should be tax deductible as well?
The fact that we pay federal income tax in no way supports the conclusion that municipal taxes should be exempt. It has always been an important principle of our income tax law that expenses in connection with property for personal use are not deductible, whereas those which are paid by a landlord are deductible because they affect business income.
I believe that we must look at the question of equity for renters. Property owners do receive an advantage over renters because the equity in their home or property is exempt from capital gains tax and, indeed, during the past few years when property values have risen rapidly this capital gain has been an important source of income for the retirement of many people, and has not been subject to tax. The tax deduction mentioned in this motion would again treat home owners preferentially. It would tend to favour the more affluent since they are more likely to own homes and have more valuable homes.
Regarding the position of landlords, it may be argued that landlords receive preferential treatment since they may deduct property taxes when computing their taxable income. However, the rental income of landlords is taxable and municipal
April 12, 1984

property taxes, like other costs incurred while earning the landlord's business income, are properly deductible. The same does not apply to home owners and renters nor does it apply, of course, to the personal residence of a landlord. He can deduct the property taxes for the rest of his development, but for his own personal residence he cannot deduct those municipal taxes.
It might be argued that in some way renters could be allowed to claim the property tax deduction instead of landlords. This would no doubt result in landlords raising rents in order to compensate for their increased income tax liabilities. As a result, many renters would be left probably no better off, and those renters who pay no income tax because of their low incomes would be worse off. They would be paying higher rent but getting no tax advantage.
If, for some reason, it was decided to allow both renters and landlords to claim the deduction, the result would be an undue incentive for rental housing.
With respect to the cost of the proposal, it is estimated that full income tax deductibility of municipal taxes paid by home owners could cost some $1 billion in forgone federal tax revenues. The cost could rise to approximately SI.5 billion if the right to this deduction was also granted to those households-more than one-third of the total-who rent their homes, assuming landlords were also allowed to deduct the cost against their rental income. I suggest that is a significant figure. We are talking about $1.5 billion. If it is forgone because of the deductibility of one's personal municipal taxes or the resulting personal municipal taxes passed through to the renter, of course it has to be collected from other sources by the federal Government.
The consequences are that the federal deficit is increased by these very substantial amounts, the federal Government services to Canadians are reduced or an equivalent amount is made up by increasing federal taxes in another direction.
The motion implies that some further incentive is needed to increase home ownership, since it calls the present tax system an impediment to this goal. There is no strong evidence that the tax system is an impediment to home ownership. Approximately two-thirds of Canadian households own their own homes. This proposal would be a windfall gain for those households already owning their homes. It would be no incentive for them. Thus it would be a costly, inefficient form of incentive for home ownership. There is already a major program of incentive for home ownership in the form of registered home ownership savings plans.
I suggest we should look at the effects on other levels of government. The benefits to home owners from this proposal could be eroded in two ways: First, it would be easier for municipal councils to increase local taxes, knowing that the federal Government would absorb part of the added burden through the income tax deduction. This would mean a weakening of an important discipline on local governments by encouraging wasteful spending. It would also be an unneces-
Income Tax Act
sary and undesirable intrusion in provincial and municipal affairs.
Second, provincial Governments might well decide to take advantage of the situation by reducing their own transfers to the municipalities. They are already being reduced. The net result could thus be simply a transfer of fiscal resources from federal to provincial Governments with little or no benefit to the taxpayers. It would favour home owners as compared to renters, unless some way could be found of extending the deductibility to renters. It is a move which is not advocated by this motion.
It would favour the more affluent as compared to lower income families, since their tax savings from a deduction is greater as a result of their higher tax bracket. The deduction for the wealthy would likely be higher as well, since they live in better houses and pay higher property taxes.
There would also be inequities among provinces in the benefits provided. The level of property taxes varies significantly among provinces due to differences in methods of financing local Governments. Some provincial Governments finance a larger share of municipal services than do other provinces. The home owner in such a province would pay lower municipal taxes but higher provincial taxes. The deduction proposed today would discriminate against such home owners.
A number of provinces have instituted various forms of relief for property taxes. These amounted to a total of approximately $1 billion in tax credits in 1982. The introduction of a federal tax credit would lead to further interprovincial inequities. For instance, in the Province of Ontario there are significant tax credits for senior citizens. In some cases, I am told, this results in practically no municipal taxes being paid. This would further add to that. I doubt that it would really provide the equity that we should be seeking in any move in this direction.
In view of these complexities, it seems more reasonable to leave responsibility for municipal taxes to the provinces, which have the constitutional responsibility to determine the appropriate degree and nature of any tax relief for municipal ratepayers. While this proposal may seem to have a great deal of appeal at first glance, there are many complexities relating to it, such as equity between lenders and home owners, to home owners who own their homes and those who are paying them off, and many inequities between provinces which provide greater or lesser transfer payments. It seems to me that before such a project or proposal is adopted, it requires a great deal more consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak very briefly on this subject. It is my intention to support the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley). I believe it is a very sensible proposal and one which would do much to stimulate home ownership and housing construction in Canada. I congratulate the Member for bringing this forward today. It is not a new idea, however. It was an integral part of the proposals to stimulate home ownership and housing construction by the

April 12, 1984
Income Tax Act
Clark government in 1979. It is indeed unfortunate that that government did not stay in office long enough to implement some of its very worthwhile proposals in this field.
I could not help but rise to my feet when I heard the presentation by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). He read a speech that had evidently been prepared for him by departmental officials, in which he said that the matter had been considered in great detail and discarded. From listening to his speech, I cannot see how any great deal of consideration had been given to these eminent proposals. For instance, he said that the costs of the scheme would be some $1.5 billion. If I listened correctly to the first Member who spoke, he did not propose full implementation. His idea was to allow a partial deduction. For instance, 50 per cent would be some $750 million.
We can look at other areas where the Government is spending money. It has spent $1.5 billion in Canadair and will likely spend more in order to "save"-we do not know if it will-just a few thousand jobs at best. The same type of approach has been taken toward de Havilland with $350 million going into that company. We know that it will have to sink more money into it in the years to come. When we contrast the proposed tax expenditure, or money that the Government will no longer collect, with moneys that the Government is spending on these other porkbarrel type programs and expenditures, it will be seen that the amount of funds involved is something quite reasonable. I do not believe that we can write it off out of hand without studying it in the detail that it deserves, and the detail into which evidently the Hon. Member for Algoma has not gone.
In a typical Liberal fashion, Sir, he says to contrast the simple straightforward proposal put forth by the Hon. Member for Don Valley West with the Registered Home Ownership Program presently in the Government's portfolio of crazy ideas. The RHOSP Program is a typical Liberal program. It is very difficult, confining and very bureaucratic. It necessitates Government taking money, giving it back again, and very detailed treatment as regards taxation. It is something typically bureaucratic, the type of thing you would expect from the Liberals, whereas the proposals coming from this side of the House have been very simple and straightforward, a simple deduction contained on one line of the income tax form. One does not need a doctorate in accounting to be able to Figure it out. Everyone can understand it. It is a great idea, Sir.
The proposal has been criticized by Hon. Members on the other side in that it perhaps would encourage municipalities to increase their taxation. That is not necessarily bad if they could do that without increasing the effect on the taxpayer. Municipalities are strapped for funds. They have very limited areas of revenue generation available to them. Nearly all of their revenue comes from property taxation, and they have worthwhile things to do. I suggest that were municipalities able to collect a little more money through the jurisditional
area given to them, property taxes in particular, then they would not have to be scrounging to provincial or federal Governments. They would be their own, men, so to speak, and I would like to see that happen.
I do not like the idea which is so prevalent among Hon. Members on the other side, that the federal Government should get in there and tax everything and not allow any room for the other two levels of government. The federal Government takes everything, then gives back to the provinces and to the municipalities, either directly or through the provinces, some of this tax money. In my opinion, there should be a proper amount of tax room for all three levels of government sufficient for them to carry out their duties and responsibilities in their jurisdictional fields without having to go to other levels of government.
There was a suggestion made by the Hon. Member for Algoma that such a program might disproportionately favour people in the middle-income bracket. The Hon. Members opposite always pretend that they are the great friends of the poor and are not really concerned with the average Canadian or the person who would like to have a little higher income than he or she does at the present time. I do not believe this is a strong objection to the proposal.
I understand that in the Province of Ontario where there is a provincial system of rebates for municipal taxes, it has managed to address this problem. It does it in a way and manner which is both fair to the owner and to the tenant.
In the Northwest Territories where there is a territorial rebate of certain municipal taxes, that is done in a simple way, but in a way which is quite fair. Rebates are given at a rate of 50 per cent of the municipal taxation up to a limit. So if one has a 4,000 square foot home and is obliged to pay $3,000 or $4,000 a year or more in municipal taxes, one cannot get 50 per cent of $4,000 but just 50 per cent of a certain amount up to a maximum. It is not entirely equitable but it is reasonable. Everyone sees that an attempt has been made at fairness and there are no real complaints about that. So I do not really agree with the objections put forward at all.
My final comment is that, in my opinion, it is a form of double taxation. It is the same type of double taxation which we now have in the case of mining or oil and gas companies. There is no deduction made for provincial royalties paid when it comes to computing federal income tax. It is that type of approach to life which makes it seem that the Government, in its wish to get more and more revenue, is not willing to take into account anything which might be fair and reasonable if it would decrease revenues which it might otherwise obtain.
We think we are good at thinking up new taxes here, but taxes have been around for thousands and thousands of years. In ancient Alexandria in Egypt 2,000 or more years ago they had thought up nearly every method of taxation and revenue raising that we have today. However, they thought of one more, and I do not really like to bring this to the attention of the Government because it might very well adopt it. However, what they did in ancient Alexandria, Sir, is make it necessary, after you paid all of your taxes, to get a tax receipt to show to
April 12, 1984

the enforcers that the taxes had been paid. Someone had the bright idea of a tax payable on getting your tax receipt, a tax on taxes paid. I just throw that out in case Hon. Members opposite might want to raise another few thousand dollars from hard-working and already oppressed Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a lot of feeling that I enter into this debate today. Having been involved in the 1979 election and believing that it was not a fair tax at that time, 1 have no notion of being in support of it today. This motion tells us a great deal about the relative priorities of those who would advocate its adoption. It would cost the federal Treasury approximately $1 billion in lost tax revenues to carry out this proposal. That means the Government would have to find that much money in some way to provide this kind of tax benefit to Canadians who own their own homes. This could be done by increasing the deficit or borrowing the money at a time when both the Government and the Official Opposition favour reducing the deficit.
If this tax benefit were not provided by deficit financing, then it would be necessary to reduce other government expenditures, or increase other taxes to offset the cost. There is no free lunch, Mr. Speaker. One billion dollars is a great deal of money to offset. It would take some deep cuts in government services to Canadians or a substantial increase in the burden carried by taxpayers.
But let us assume that we can free up $1 billion in resources available to Government to spend where it thinks the need is greatest. What this motion argues, by inference at least, is that the $1 billion should be spent on Canadians who own their homes. It has been said that "to govern is to choose". We do not have unlimited resources. We have to choose our priorities. I believe we must help those who really need it most.
The last two Budgets set out a number of major priorities and announced a series of initiatives to meet them. Their goal is to build a strong and lasting expansion of the economy that will increase employment in Canada. I mention last year's Budget because its Special Recovery Program was planned for the medium term. Half of it was in the form of direct federal spending to provide new capital facilities that will increase competitiveness and generate new jobs. The other half was in the form of incentives for private investment to improve the competitive strength and job-creating capacity of the private sector. The Special Recovery Capital Projects will have their peak impact-estimated at $1.1 billion-in the new fiscal year just begun.
This year's Budget dealt with other high priorities: expansion of the youth opportunity fund to improve employment prospects for young people, new initiatives in employee profitsharing plans, tax simplification for small businesses, pension
Income Tax Act
reform, and increased security for home owners in the mortgage market. These are priorities of Government policy which have an important call on the available financial resources.
Do supporters of this motion claim that a billion-dollar tax benefit to home owners commands an equal or higher priority when it comes to allocating scarce fiscal resources? What would be gained by allowing home owners to deduct their municipal taxes from income subject to federal income tax? The motion states that this action would remove an impediment to homeownership for the average Canadian. I suggest that the level of municipal taxes has not been an impediment to a great many Canadians in deciding to become home owners, and the fact that two-thirds of Canadian households own their homes is an indication of that. Yet these are the people who would receive the bulk of the proposed tax benefit.
If we want to spend $1 billion as an incentive for Canadians to become home owners for the first time, surely the incentive should be targeted at them, not at those who have shown they no longer need that incentive. In spending Government money on new programs or tax incentives, it is vital that the money be used in the most efficient way possible. That means applying the incentive at the margin, to influence future decisions, and not using most of the financial resources to reward decisions that have been taken in the past.
Another important weakness in this proposal is that it would introduce a most regressive aspect to our income tax law. A basic principle of tax law is that citizens should be asked to pay taxes according to their ability to pay. Wealthier taxpayers should be expected to carry a proportionately heavier tax burden than those who are on lower incomes.
There is a great deal to be said in favour of leaving the responsibilitity for local taxes in its present form. It exercises a certain discipline in that people are directly responsible for their community expenditures. Having spent ten years of my life in municipal government, I believe that they really know where their dollars come from and where they go. I wish to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity of putting on the record a few of those thoughts.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak on this Bill, I cannot help but relate back to the proposal of the Opposition when they were in government and the home owner's interest deductibility which would have cost the Government of Canada approximately $3.5 billion. It is not easy to find a valid rationale for adopting the proposal urged in this motion. Should it be in the form of an incentive for home ownership? The motion suggests that, since it describes the present tax structure as being an impediment to Canadians owning their own homes. Should it be done in order to correct a great defect in the tax structure? That seems to be the position taken in this motion, since it talks of correcting "an unfair form of double taxation". Or is it intended simply as a transfer to benefit home owners? It certainly looks as though that would be the result, if not the motive, and we should consider whether such a transfer is justifiable.

April 12, 1984
Income Tax Act
Let us look at the question of providing an added incentive to home ownership. The cost of this proposal in reduced federal tax revenues could be about $1 billion, assuming full deduction of municipal property taxes. That is a pretty rich benefit and the sponsor of the motion apparently recognizes that since the motion suggests there might be some limitation in the form of a ceiling on the amount of property taxes which could be deducted.
It is hard to accept the argument that the present nondeductibility of property taxes is an impediment to homeown-ership. About two-thirds of Canadian households live in their own homes-a remarkably high percentage by any standard. Therefore, if we are to regard this proposal as an incentive to homeownership, it clearly would be a very inefficient and wasteful one. Almost all of the tax benefits would go to those who now own their homes. And in any event there is little evidence that the level of municipal taxation is acting as a deterrent to those who might want to become first-time homeowners.
If we want to devote government financial resources to encouraging people to become homeowners, it makes sense that any incentive be directed specifically towards them and not diverted to existing homeowners. That is precisely the purpose of the existing tax provision for contributions into registered homeownership savings plans. The RHOSP tax benefit involves a cost to the federal treasury in forgone tax revenues of around $100 million a year. At last count some 540,000 Canadians were contributing to their RHOSP accounts. I should remind the House of the change to the RHOSP program introduced in the Recovery budget of April last year, allowing taxpayers extra tax deduction by topping up their RHOSP contributions to the maximum $10,000 in order to buy newly-built homes before the end of 1984.
In addition there are substantial amounts provided through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to a number of major housing programs to assist Canadians-including home renovation and rehabilitation, the financing of social housing for low-income households, and rental subsidies for households needing housing assistance. It must be obvious that this kind of approach is a far more effective way of using federal tax resources to improve the housing of Canadians. I would like to turn now to another argument made in support of the proposed motion-the idea that an income tax deduction for municipal property taxes would correct what the motion calls "an unfair form of double taxation". That is an intriguing and puzzling argument. It is true that homeowners pay their municipal taxes out of their income after paying federal and provincial income tax. But the same applies to payments of every form of tax that is not income tax-sales tax, customs tariffs, excise taxes, dog taxes, liquor taxes. Do all of these amount to double taxation? Are we to provide for income tax deductions for all of these other taxes as well, on grounds they constitute double taxation? That seems to be the logic of this motion.
I suggest that homeowners view their municipal property taxes as payments which finance essential local services. I doubt very much that they see these taxes as representing
double taxation. I agree that property taxes are paid in so-called "after-tax" dollars-after payment of income tax- but the same can be said for every other purchase of goods and services. It is a far stretch to call this double taxation.
We must conclude that this proposal cannot be justified either as an incentive to homeownership, or as a necessary correction to some supposed problem of double taxation. We are left, therefore, with trying to justify the motion as a worthwhile and necessary fiscal transfer to homeowners. Can one argue that this is really a high priority area for the allocation of as much as $1 billion in federal government resources?
We hear much from the Opposition about the need to reduce the federal deficit, so one can perhaps assume that the sponsor of the motion would not want to increase the deficit by another $1 billion.
That leaves two alternative approaches. If we are to offset the cost of this proposal by reducing expenditures in other areas, the supporters of this proposal should take the responsibility of specifying which federal services should be cut. Or else they should make clear what tax increases they advocate in order to make up the lost revenue.
If we are going to find $1 billion by some general increase in tax revenues, the implication is clear: it means that taxpayers as a whole will be asked to subsidize homeowners. You would be asking families who cannot afford to own their own homes to provide tax assistance for those who do. Since home owners are generally at higher income levels than those who rent, this means seriously regressive taxation.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ISSUANCE OF LAY-OFF NOTICES TO WORKERS. (B) CONTRACTING PRACTICES-EFFECT ON RAILWAY EMPLOYEES
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ISSUANCE OF LAY-OFF NOTICES TO WORKERS. (B) CONTRACTING PRACTICES-EFFECT ON RAILWAY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about two weeks ago when workers in the western shops of the CPR in Winnipeg learned that a number of their workers would be laid off permanently they sent a telegram to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) protesting the lay-offs and urging the Minister to take some action to alleviate the hardships which would arise. Yesterday I brought this to the attention of the Minister and asked him to look into it. I also informed him
April 12, 1984

that I had learned two days ago that a number of workers in the car shop in Winnipeg had been told that they would be laid off shortly. I asked the Minister to take action. Of course the Minister gave the usual reply that as a result of the passage of the legislation ending the Crow rate agreement there would be a substantial increase in the number of people working across the country and in Winnipeg.
I put it to the Minister yesterday, and I do so again today, that 57 full-time jobs are being terminated in Winnipeg in the diesel shop, the power house and the wheel shop operation. A number of workers who have worked for CPR in Montreal and Toronto are being moved to Winnipeg. This will cause a good deal of dislocation to them and their families. I also pointed out to the Minister that lay-offs are now taking place in the car shop.
I would like to remind the House what the Minister said on March 25, 1982. He said:
We are talking about the kind of investment that will restore the urban centres of western Canada to their pre-eminence as transportation centres. We are talking about the creation of employment across Canada, from the steel mills in Sydney to the locomotive shops in Quebec and Ontario and the major urban centres of western Canada. The change in the Crow rate will have multiple benefits for every community across Canada. It will create employment.
That is the question to which I am trying to get an answer from the Minister. Where are these jobs? Why are these people being laid off?
The Minister can say that the new programs have not started yet and that it will take some time. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian Pacific is one of the largest, if not the largest corporation in Canada. In 1983 it had gross revenues of $2,430 million and a net income of $184 million, an increase over 1982 of almost 50 per cent. Canadian Pacific is a big, sound, profitable corporation. It got to the position it is in, Mr. Speaker, because of the benefits it received from the people of Canada. Since it was started it has received billions of dollars in grants, hundreds of thousands of acres of land, and untold mineral wealth. If this corporation cannot see its way to carry a few of its employees, for whom there is no work right now, until the time when they and the Minister have assured the people of Canada and their workers that they are going to expand their work force, that says something which is not very commendable about both the CPR and the Minister of Transport.
My second question to the Minister of Transport concerns another issue which has come to light with regard to both the CNR and the CPR. They are continuing and expanding a policy of contracting out work which they started some years ago. When I asked the Minister about that and urged him to do something about it, he said he would talk to the CPR. But he said, "you know, the railways have to be more efficient." What efficiency means when you put the word "efficiency', together with the words "contracting out" is that the railway lays off fulltime employees, permanent employees, who because they are permanent employees and because they are represented by unions have been able to negotiate a decent wage, working conditions and benefits for themselves. What contracting out does is to get rid of those employees and
Adjournment Debate
replace them with people who are casual employees who work only when the company has a specific job to do. They work for much lower wages and do not get the benefits and so on which permanent employees get. Studies have been done in Toronto, Windsor, and my own city of Winnipeg which indicate that contracting out services are not as efficiently done as work done by fulltime experienced employees. Contracting out services suffer from high turnover and poor workplace safety standards, and these jobs are often done at minimum wage and produce high returns for the agency-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-ISSUANCE OF LAY-OFF NOTICES TO WORKERS. (B) CONTRACTING PRACTICES-EFFECT ON RAILWAY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other industrial and commercial businesses, CP Rail must occasionally redistribute its human resources and adjust its hiring operations according to the variations in the demand for its product, that is, rail transportation. The most recent staff reductions planned by the CPR in Winnipeg are the result of decisions reached by the directors to maintain an efficient and profitable service. I would like to emphasize that, as a private enterprise, the CPR is required to make profits for its shareholders.
In 1983, in spite of lay-offs and recalls of employees in various occupational groups, there was a net increase in the number of CPR shop employees in Winnipeg. If the current economic recovery keeps up, the opportunities for permanent jobs should continue to improve.
I would add that the temporary shop employees hired by CP Rail were warned at the time of their hiring about this situation so they would be sure not to quit more permanent jobs. In addition to that, the collective agreements covering the laid-off permanent employees protect them against excessive hardship.
The CPR alone has undertaken to allocate something like $450 million to equipment projects in 1984. The purpose of this record high expenditure program is to increase its capacity to move ever-increasing freight volumes. The program flows from the new Western Grain Transportation Act which, for the first time in years, requires payment for the movement of grain.
The CNR and the CPR have initiated many projects which will improve their ability to move the products of Western Canada. As the Minister has said: "We are embarking on a major economic development". The companies are now contracting for purchases and projects which will benefit nearly all the regions of Canada.
The purpose of work distribution by railway companies is not to avoid paying unionized workers. Companies bid for the equipment projects through the normal channels, and I can

April 12, 1984
Adjournment Debate
assure the Hon. Member that selection is made on the basis of price and quality of the proposals and not of the fact that the workers are unionized or not. On the other hand, both the CNR and the CPR have found out that most major contracts have been awarded to companies whose workers are unionized. In some cases, service contracts, such as herbicide spraying and cleaning services, have been awarded to small local companies whose employees are not unionized when they were the only bidders or those were the only services provided.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SIZE OF LABOUR FORCE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION. (B) USE OF UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUNDS TO RETRAIN WORKERS

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SIZE OF LABOUR FORCE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION. (B) USE OF UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUNDS TO RETRAIN WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 take advantage of this adjournment debate to correct for the record some of the outrageously misleading statements of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts). I specifically refer to a question I put to the Minister on April 10, 1984, which can be found at page 2899 of Hansard. My question was prompted by the public musings of the Minister in Calgary, Alberta last week.
On Friday last, the unemployment figures were released by Statistics Canada. On that occasion the Minister, who should have been in the House to answer for the increase in the unemployment rate, was musing publicly in Calgary that the reason unemployment had gone up was that more people participated in the labour force. The actual fact was that the participation rate had gone down while the unemployment rate had continued to escalate for three months. So much for the Minister's knowledge of the labour force and the labour force survey.
The second thing he said in Calgary last Friday was that in his opinion more unemployment insurance funds should be targeted toward manpower training as opposed to income maintenance. He is the Minister responsible for unemployment insurance. When he finally came into the House on Tuesday, we put questions to him. I have referred to these questions.
I asked the Minister, if he is the Minister responsible for unemployment insurance and if he believes that more unemployment insurance funds should go into training as opposed to income maintenance, why does he not do something about it? That was the question. It is there for anybody to see. The Minister's answer, as I said, was outrageously misleading. He said:
The answer is, of course, that we are. That is exactly what Section 38 and Section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act now permits . .. That is what we are doing to the extent of something like $1 billion a year.
The Minister went on to say facetiously:
Once again the Hon. Member has shown his profound lack of knowledge of what the facts of the situation are.
The Minister has shown once again his profound lack of knowledge of what the facts are. Canada faces one of the greatest challenges in this modern time; that is, the training of
our unemployed and the training of our work force to cope with technological change. There are many thousands of young people unemployed, a half million. Many people today are under-employed, especially women. Eighty per cent of the service sector is made up of women. They will be left behind unless we make provision now to train these people.
What are the facts? When the Minister made that statement in the House I checked with his office and then I checked the Estimates. I find that the Minister was wrong on all counts. Let us look at the current Estimates for 1984-85.
Under manpower training we find $259 million of the unemployment insurance fund targeted for training. That represents about 2.5 per cent of the total unemployment insurance paid out in this country. In trying to explain himself today, the Minister said he was not only talking about manpower training, but he was also talking about job creation. The record implies clearly that he was not talking about job creation but manpower training. Even if he was, the fact is that on checking the records we find that under the current Estimates only $207 million was targeted under UI for job-creation purposes. That is still only half of what the Minister said was being spent, if we take his word today that he really meant not only training but job creation as well.
The Minister does not know what he is talking about. He is preoccupied with other things. He is preoccupied with a losing campaign to save his credibility as a Minister, because we know he is not going anywhere in terms of the Liberal leadership of this country. Now he obviously has to do something about his waning credibility.
In his reply to me, incredibly he indicated for example, and I quote from page 2899 of Hansard:
That is exactly what Section 38 and Section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act now permit.
Section 38 has absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with manpower training. There is not one cent being spent under Section 38. He obviously meant Section 37. Under Section 37 of the Act, only $25,000 is being spent to retrain some 50 workers. The rest is being spent under Section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is an expenditure of $259 million a year.
We pay out almost $1 billion a month in unemployment insurance in this country. People who draw these benefits should be able to use them to be retrained; to be trained for new jobs, to be trained to cope with new technology, and be trained in the use of computers. We should be using the unemployment insurance fund to train women to meet the challenges of the new technology, to train the half million young people who will be left behind if we do not do something about training them now to handle the jobs with, hopefully, a little more emphasis on research and development and productivity, the jobs that will be created in the future if we can get our economy back on the rails.
This is a very serious matter. We have a right to expect that the Minister of the Crown responsible for training, employ-
April 12, 1984

ment, manpower and unemployment insurance would not only be here but that he would be well informed. Not only is he not here, but obviously he is ill informed. He is either ill informed, misinformed or deliberately trying to mislead the Canadian public. I know the Minister would not do that. I cannot accuse him of doing that, so he must be misinformed. Either way he stands indicted for incompetence.
