subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SIZE OF LABOUR FORCE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION. (B) USE OF UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUNDS TO RETRAIN WORKERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is easy to pick a particular month and compare it to the most current month and draw whatever conclusions one wants. The fact is, as previously stated, employment growth on an annual basis has been relatively favourable in comparison to labour force growth. Using the latest 12 months or the latest quarter compared to the corresponding one a year ago gives a more clear indication of the true situation. For instance, on a year-to-year basis, the absolute increase in employment between April 1983 and March 1984 was 242,000 while the labour force grew by 222,000. Comparing the first quarter of 1983 with the first quarter of 1984, employment grew at an annual rate of 334,000 while the labour force grew at an annual rate of 183,000. It is clear therefore that while the Government is still not satisfied with the high level of unemployment, jobs are being created at a faster rate than the growth of the labour force.

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-ELIGIBILITY OF MARRIED WOMEN
CANADA PENSION PLAN-ELIGIBILITY OF MARRIED WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my participation in today's late show flows from my intervention during Question Period yesterday. I have to admit that my intervention arose from a certain degree of anger and utter frustration because of a question from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney). He threatened the Government with the usual defeat because, he said, we keep attaching a price tag or condition to any help that we might give to farmers or fishermen. On second thought, I felt I did not have to apologize for that anger I felt or the frustration. I felt it reflected very accurately the anger and frustration of the people who have put the farmers and the fishermen in their jobs, that is the wives.
We are all politicians in this House. I agree that probably the Leader of the Opposition is reacting to a strong lobby on the part of western farmers in particular. I do not fault the farmers for having made that lobby. They were probably putting forward their own legitimate claims. I do fault the Leader of the Opposition for his insensitivity to the fact that the people who need his help most are very often the inarticulate, the needy, those who cannot afford to present this lobby. Very often that is the housewife of Canada. Until these voices can be heard, regardless of the amount of money and regardless of their ability to articulate, we are not in a very good democracy. We have to admit that. It is our duty as representatives of all the people in Canada to make sure that we are attuned to the silent voice, which very often is the most needy. This is so, particularly when it comes to the plight of farm wives.
Adjournment Debate
A few years ago, I was privileged to represent Canada at a symposium for rural women of America in Washington. It occurred to me that Canada could well do likewise and call a conference of the rural women of Canada to find out their particular problems.
Rural women do have problems which are different from those of women in urban centres. Obviously, one of the problems is isolation. Another is the amount of sheer hard work that must be done. Few city dwellers like myself will not admit that the work done by rural women is at least three times as hard as the work done by most men. For those rural women and for housewives in the city I am not asking so much for financial gain, but I am asking that a degree of dignity and justice be afforded them and that their work be recognized. The only way dignity and justice can be given to these women is by allowing them to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan.
The inclusion of housewives in the pension scheme would be a highly significant innovation which, to some extent, would recognize the economic worth of raising a family. As well, it would provide an element of financial independence for elderly unemployed women.
This idea is not a novel one, Mr. Speaker. For instance, such a program has already been adopted in Germany and France. In 1978, I had the Library of Parliament research a paper for me. I have been pursuing this question since my first election to the House in 1974. We have made some progress but not enough.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women has asked that housewives be allowed to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. More recently, our own parliamentary task force, with all-Party agreement, recommended that a homemaker pension be available to those who, in any year, work only or mainly in the home to care for a spouse, a child under 18 or a dependent and infirm adult relative living in the home.
I would like to repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I am not only asking for money. Money could be provided as, under certain circumstances; it is already being provided by the OAS and the GIS. I am asking for the recognition of the work done by these women throughout our country, and I am asking that they be accorded the justice and dignity they deserve.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-ELIGIBILITY OF MARRIED WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has been particularly attentive to the needs of women in formulating its action plan for pension reform which was released in the Budget of February 15. Before providing some details on the Budget proposals that will benefit women, I would like to point out that farmers' wives are already able to participate in the Canada Pension Plan if they work in the family business. As well, wives who work in the paid labour force do contribute to the Canada Pension Plan.

April 12, 1984
Adjournment Debate
The Government announced an impressive list of proposals that will be of particular help to women. Bills to enact these proposals are now being drafted and will be introduced as soon as possible. Elon. Members will then be asked to ensure speedy passage of these bills so that their benefits will be felt at an early date.
Let me remind Hon. Members of the proposals to help women which are included in the Budget. These include a $50 per month increase in the Guaranteed Income Supplement for single pensioners. This proposal will benefit 750,000 elderly people, three-quarters of whom are women, and will ensure that they can lead a decent life. They include as well improvements to the Canada Pension Plan to ensure that survivor benefits are not terminated upon remarriage, that pension credits are split upon marriage breakdown and that pensions are split at age 65. These proposals will provide retirement income to women in their own right.
In addition, there is reform of private pension plans to ensure inflation protection, vesting after two years and splitting of pension credits upon marriage breakdown. There is improved survivor benefits, equal benefits for men and women, greater membership in private pension plans, major tax improvements to encourage retirement income and better information in respect of both public and private pension plans. Taken together, these proposals will ensure that working
women receive in the future a much better deal from the pension system.
The Government has already sought the approval of provinces for changes to the Canada Pension Plan, and there is every indication that provinces will agree to their speedy enactment. Provinces have also been asked to reform private pension plans falling under their jurisdiction, and the federal Government will be working to achieve Canada-wide reforms.
While these are in themselves major reforms of the pension system, the Government is also committed to discuss later this year further improvements to the Canada Pension Plan. The issues which will be discussed with them include whether or not homemakers who work in the home should be covered under the CPP, survivors and disability benefits and the financing of the Plan. These are complex and difficult issues which will require careful consideration. The implementation of any major changes will also require consent of the provinces. I can therefore give the Hon. Member every assurance that the Government is fully aware of the matter which has been raised and is working diligently to ensure that elderly women do not live in poverty.
